## Chapter 6

# An End-to-End Deep Learning Framework for Accurate Tumor Detection and Segmentation in Brain MRI Scans

A. V. Kalpana

[![Orcid Image](image/orcid-logo.png)https://orcid.org/0000-0003-2289-4968](https://orcid.org/0000-0003-2289-4968)

SRM Institute of Science and Technology, India

B. Bharathi

[![Orcid Image](image/orcid-logo.png)https://orcid.org/0009-0001-1068-996X](https://orcid.org/0009-0001-1068-996X)

R.M.K. Engineering College, India

### ABSTRACT

This chapter presents an automated biomedical image classification system, HBDL-FBTA (Hybrid Bio-inspired Deep Learning with Fusion Brain Tumor Analysis), focused on brain tumors—abnormal cell growths in the brain or surrounding tissues that require early, accurate detection for effective treatment. The HBDL-FBTA employs pre-processing to enhance image quality, Swin-UNet-based segmentation for precise region delineation, and fusion-based feature extraction for robust feature acquisition. It uses Humpback Whale Optimization with Simulated Annealing (HSSA) for parameter tuning and a Gated Recurrent Unit (GRU) for reliable classification. Simulations on benchmark datasets, including BraTS2017, demonstrate superior performance, achieving accuracies of 94.51% on ISIC 2017 and 95.38% on ISIC 2020 datasets. Future work will focus on evaluating computational complexity on large-scale datasets, integrating multi-modal imaging data, and developing interpretable deep learning models to enhance clinical adoption and reliability.

### 1\. INTRODUCTION

A wide variety of methods and strategies are used in the vast field of biomedical image analysis to extract, process, and interpret pertinent information from biomedical images ([S. Nazir et. al, 2023](#979-8-3693-9816-6.ch006.bits-pdf.xhtml#_idTextAnchor385)). It plays a crucial part in clinical practice, medical research, and healthcare administration (M. Obayya et.al, 2022). The duties of automatically labeling or classifying medical images according to their content are referred to as biomedical image classification (S. Chakraborty et. al). Due of the abundance of medical imaging data and the potential for Deep Learning (DL) techniques to assist medical professionals in identifying illnesses and making treatment decisions, the field has attracted a lot of attention recently ([M. Di Giammarco et. al, 2022](#979-8-3693-9816-6.ch006.bits-pdf.xhtml#_idTextAnchor380)). Medical image analysis seeks to provide radiologists and doctors with instruments for efficient diagnostic and therapeutic procedures ([J. Yang et. al, 2023](#979-8-3693-9816-6.ch006.bits-pdf.xhtml#_idTextAnchor390)). Medical imaging tools such as CT, MRI, and X-ray can provide anatomical and functional information on diseases and anomalies inside the body without causing any damage ([J. Zhu et. al, 2023](#979-8-3693-9816-6.ch006.bits-pdf.xhtml#_idTextAnchor391)). Processing is necessary to retrieve meaningful data from medical images since they contain flaws, artifacts, and confounding information (if any exist) ([F. Li et. al, 2023](#979-8-3693-9816-6.ch006.bits-pdf.xhtml#_idTextAnchor384)). Medical applications have benefited greatly from the contributions of image processing techniques; for example, image-guided surgery, segmentation of images, and registration of images are widely used in medical diagnosis and treatment (S. Maqsood et. al, 2023). DL approaches significantly outperform human professionals in certain domains, such as medical imaging. Massive datasets are used by DL algorithms to forecast complicated tasks.

In tasks involving picture interpretation in Computer Vision (CV), the DL approach has achieved a significantly greater degree of accuracy ([A. Shrivastava et. al, 2022](#979-8-3693-9816-6.ch006.bits-pdf.xhtml#_idTextAnchor389)). The most efficient type of neural networks for information analysis in a grid-form architecture are convolutional deep neural networks (CNNs) (D. Sharma et. al, 203). The most effective method for medical imaging analysis in recent years has been the DL model, particularly Deep CNN (DCNN) ([S. Dash et. al, 2023](#979-8-3693-9816-6.ch006.bits-pdf.xhtml#_idTextAnchor379)). When it comes to picture classification tasks, Deep Neural Networks (DNNs) perform significantly better than other Artificial Intelligence (AI) technologies and can often outperform human domain experts. Concern over the use of AI technology for imaging segmentation and classification in biomedical applications has grown (K. VanHorn et. al, 2022). Although encoder-decoder converter methods are advised, CNN is a more contemporary paradigm for picture classification and segmentation ([S. Patel et. al, 2022](#979-8-3693-9816-6.ch006.bits-pdf.xhtml#_idTextAnchor387)) ([Aamir et al., 2019](#979-8-3693-9816-6.ch006.bits-pdf.xhtml#_idTextAnchor372)).

Hybrid Bio-inspired Deep Learning - Fusion based Brain Tumor Analysis (HBDL-FBTA) is presented in this paper. The pictures are first preprocessed and segmented using the Swin-UNet model by the HBDL-FBTA approach. The Xception and Residual Network (ResNet) models then perform the merger of several DL-based feature extractors. Additionally, a Hybrid Whale Optimization Algorithm (WOA) with Adaptive Particle Swarm Optimization (APSO) called HWOA\_APSO was used to choose the best hyperparameters for the DL models. The recognition and classification of biomedical images was finally accomplished by utilizing the gated recurrent unit (GRU) method. The HBDL-FBTA algorithm's superior performance is demonstrated by a comprehensive simulation examination.

#### Figure 1. Global Healthcare AI market revenue 2022-2032

![](image/979-8-3693-9816-6.ch006.f01.png)

Through its revolutionary impact on patient care, diagnosis, and treatment, artificial intelligence (also known as AI) is redefining the healthcare sector. AI analyzes vast amounts of medical data, such as imaging tests, patient records, and scientific literature, using sophisticated algorithms as well as machine learning approaches to produce insightful results that improve clinical decision-making. In order to enhance patient outcomes, machine learning models are especially good at finding patterns in data, forecasting the course of diseases, and creating individualized treatment regimens.

Radiology, pathological conditions, and dermatology are among the medical imaging specialties that have been greatly impacted by AI-powered tools. These tools help doctors identify anomalies more accurately and efficiently by enabling very accurate image identification. Another essential AI technology is Natural Language Processing (the NLP), which makes it easier to analyze medical literature and keeps medical practitioners abreast of the most recent findings. Virtual assistants who offer patients real-time health advice and support are also powered by NLP.

AI improves healthcare delivery in addition to diagnostics by speeding up drug discovery procedures, enabling remote patient monitoring, and using predictive analytics for population health management. AI-driven solutions can improve total healthcare efficiency by identifying at-risk individuals, forecasting future health trends, and allocating resources optimally. AI in healthcare has obstacles despite its revolutionary potential. Important issues that demand attention include data privacy concerns, the necessity of strong legal frameworks, and the significance of combining physician experience with AI capabilities. To overcome these obstacles and guarantee the safe, moral, and successful application of AI, cooperation between AI developers, medical practitioners, and legislators is crucial.

The growing importance of AI in healthcare is reflected in the global market. The market is expected to develop at an outstanding compound annual growth rate (CAGR) of 30.6% from 2022 to 2032, reaching a size of USD 280.77 billion by 2032. This quick expansion highlights the growing use of AI-powered technologies to improve healthcare systems throughout the globe, opening the door to more individualized patient care and quicker, more accurate diagnosis.

### 2\. BACKGROUND AND RELATED WORKS

An intelligent method for dividing CXR and MRI pictures into abnormal and normal classes for the initial identification of HD, COVID19, and AD that relies on ensemble DNN is examined by [Pradhan et al. (2023)](#979-8-3693-9816-6.ch006.bits-pdf.xhtml#_idTextAnchor388). CNN was used in the presented method to automatically extract features from photos, while LSTM was used as the final classifier. Additionally, the Hill-Climbing Algorithm (HCA) is used to fit the other parameters while identifying the best possible value for the CNN and LSTM hyperparameters, such as the CNN filter dimensionality and the LSTM unit counts. A novel encoded-decoded structure called DOLG-NeXt is examined by [Ahmed et al. (2023)](#979-8-3693-9816-6.ch006.bits-pdf.xhtml#_idTextAnchor374), who incorporate three key enhancements over the UNet-based variants. The authors primarily use the ConvNeXt phases driven by SE-Net as an embedded backbone to effectively extract features. Secondarily, the authors retrieve fine-grained contextual feature representation by using DOLG feature components from the decoded. For the classification of biomedical images, [Barzekar and Yu (2022)](#979-8-3693-9816-6.ch006.bits-pdf.xhtml#_idTextAnchor378) investigate a novel CNN structure called C-Net, which is made up of the concatenation of several networks. Six networks make up the first two components of the architecture, which help with feature extraction to create an inner network for benign and malignant picture classification. Mansour (2022) presents AIFM-CRC, a novel AI-based fusion technique for CRC classification and analysis. Additionally, a classification method for identifying the existence of CRC was the WOA-tuned deep SVM algorithm.

In recent research by G. Habib et. al (2020), a novel deep CNN method for classifying brain tumors was introduced. By using TL to some extent for data distillation, a revolutionary CNN technique could save the requirement to be trained from start, wasting days or weeks. Additionally, weights were created using the Gaussian initialization strategy and subsequently the ReLu activation function in order to increase the trained acceleration using different optimizer approaches. Diagonal Bilinear Interpolated Deep Residual Network (DBI-DRSN) is a novel deep feature extraction and classification method for biomedical pictures created by [Assad and Kiczales (2020)](#979-8-3693-9816-6.ch006.bits-pdf.xhtml#_idTextAnchor376) . The DBI-DRSN approach classifies the features using the DRSN approach's fine-tuning and incorporates a balance of information or features using the DBI pre-processing approach.

[Pang et al. (2019)](#979-8-3693-9816-6.ch006.bits-pdf.xhtml#_idTextAnchor386) describe a new fused CNN that combines shallow and deep layer characteristics in the given DNN structure to create an even more accurate and highly effective classification for biological images. Using biomedical pictures, [Alanazi et al. (2022)](#979-8-3693-9816-6.ch006.bits-pdf.xhtml#_idTextAnchor375) investigate an intelligent DL-allowed oral squamous cell carcinoma detection and classification (IDL-OSCDC) method. GF is used as the pre-processed step in the proposed IDL-OSCDC technique to remove noise content. Additionally, OC detection and classification were done using a DBN approach based on enhanced GOA (EGOA). The EGOA technique was used to perform the hyper-parameter tweaking of the DBN algorithm, which improves the classifier results.

The application of the red foxes heuristic optimization algorithm (RFOA) for diagnostic segmentation of images is suggested by [Jaszcz et al. (2022)](#979-8-3693-9816-6.ch006.bits-pdf.xhtml#_idTextAnchor382). With the innovative fitness function and the emphasis on equation modification, the heuristics' operation was modified for the analysis of 2D images. To overcome these difficulties, the Harris Hawks optimised convolution networks (HHOCNN) is employed by S.Z.Kurdi et.al (2023). To reduce the rate of false tumor recognition, the brain magnetic resonance (MR) picture was preprocessed, and noisy pixels were removed. The malignant area is then located using the candidate region approach. A lightweight deep learning technique for human gait identification is presented by [Khan et al. (2022)](#979-8-3693-9816-6.ch006.bits-pdf.xhtml#_idTextAnchor383). Two light pretrained models are first examined and improved in terms of adding more layers and freezing some intermediate layers. The moth-flame optimization approach improves the discriminatory correlation analysis, which can be used to complete the fusion process.

There is a significant research gap in the areas of feature extraction and hyperparameter tuning in the field of medical picture classification. Even though DL algorithms have produced excellent results in this field, feature extraction techniques specific to medical picture characteristics can yet be improved ([Guan et al., 2021](#979-8-3693-9816-6.ch006.bits-pdf.xhtml#_idTextAnchor381)). The discriminatory strength of a classification model may be enhanced via fusion-based extraction of features, which combines data from various DL techniques. Furthermore, the model performance for the medical picture classification task may be further enhanced by the methodical adjustment of hyperparameters, including those pertaining to network design and optimization strategies. The majority of current literature does not concentrate on applying metaheuristics for hyperparameter optimization. In the end, closing this research gap could lead to more reliable and accurate categorization methods, which would improve clinical evaluation and planning of treatment in the medical industry. As a result, the creation and development of the fusion-based feature extraction procedure using the ResNet and Xception models has been the main emphasis of this work. Additionally, the HSSA can be used to do the hyperparameter tuning procedure.

### 3\. THE PROPOSED METHODOLOGY

The HBDL-FBTA (Hybrid Bio-inspired Deep Learning-Based Fusing Model for Brain Tumor Analysis) method is a complete framework for automated biomedical classification of images that is presented in this article. The HBDL-FBTA approach's main objective is to precisely evaluate and categorize biological pictures for illness diagnosis, tackling important issues in contemporary healthcare diagnostics. The framework is methodically created, combining several sophisticated stages that complement one another to improve dependability and performance.

To guarantee uniform and high-quality inputs, pre-processing is the initial step, during which raw biological images are enhanced and noise-removed. In order to reduce mistakes and inconsistencies in later processing, this step is essential. After pre-processing, particular regions of interest across the images are isolated using Swin-UNet-based segmentation. By utilizing the Swin Transformer model's capacity to capture combined global and local picture features, the Swin-UNet architecture provides remarkable segmentation precision. Only the most pertinent portions of the image are examined further thanks to this segmentation.

In the subsequent stage, two cutting-edge deep learning models, Xception and Residual Network (ResNet), are used to perform fusion-based feature extraction. The framework captures complex patterns and variations in the biomedical pictures by combining the strengths of different models to extract a wide range of useful features. The framework's representational capability is greatly increased by this fusion technique, which makes it possible for it to distinguish between intricate disease features. For hyperparameter optimization, the HWOA\_APSO is used to maximize the performance of the deep learning models. By methodically adjusting the settings, this metaheuristic optimization technique makes sure the models perform to their best ability. The framework is more reliable and scenario-adaptive because to the addition of HSSA, which also improves accuracy and computing efficiency.

The Gated Recurrent Unit (GRU) algorithm is used for classification in the last stage. Recurrent neural networks (RNNs), of which GRU is a variation, excel in processing temporal and sequential data. The GRU algorithm effectively and remarkably accurately diagnoses and classifies diseases by examining the retrieved features. A comprehensive and reliable analysis of biomedical pictures is ensured by this multi-layered technique, which combines segmentation, feature extraction, optimization, and classification.

[Figure 2](#979-8-3693-9816-6.ch006.bits-pdf.xhtml#_idTextAnchor365) shows the HBDL-FBTA framework's comprehensive process, which includes each of these stages. The suggested approach shows great promise to transform biomedical image analysis by fusing cutting-edge deep learning techniques with creative metaheuristic optimization. Its potential as a potent instrument for improving diagnostic precision and efficiency in healthcare applications is highlighted by its capacity to provide accurate and trustworthy disease classification.

This paper presents a comprehensive framework for automated biomedical image classification using the HBDL-FBTA (Hybrid Meta Heuristics plus Deep Learning-Based Fusing Model for Medicinal Image Analysis) technique. The primary goal of the HBDL-FBTA technique is to accurately assess and classify biological images for the diagnosis of illness, addressing significant problems in modern healthcare diagnostics. The structure is carefully constructed, including multiple advanced phases that enhance performance and dependability.

#### Figure 2. The proposed HBDL-FBTA Framework

![](image/979-8-3693-9816-6.ch006.f02.png)

Pre-processing is the first stage to ensure consistent and high-quality inputs, where raw biological images are improved, and noise is eliminated. This phase is crucial to minimizing errors and inconsistencies in subsequent processing. Following pre-processing, Swin-UNet-based segmentation is used to separate certain regions of interest within the images. Using the ability of the Swin Transformer model to collect both local and integrated global picture features, the Swin-UNet architecture achieves exceptional segmentation accuracy. This segmentation ensures that only the most relevant areas of the image are subsequently analysed.

The next step is fusion-based feature extraction using two state-of-the-art deep learning models, Xception and Residual Network (ResNet). The framework combines the strengths of various models to extract a wide range of valuable information, capturing intricate patterns and variations in the biological images. This fusion strategy significantly improves the representational capability of the framework, allowing it to discriminate between complex illness features.

The HWOA\_APSO is used for hyperparameter optimization in order to optimize the deep learning models' performance. This metaheuristic optimization strategy ensures that the models operate as efficiently as possible by systematically modifying the settings. The use of HSSA enhances accuracy and processing efficiency while making the framework more dependable and scenario adaptive.

The Gated Recurrent Unit (GRU) algorithm is used for classification as the last step in the suggested methodology. GRU is an advanced type of Recurrent Neural Network (RNN) that excels at processing and evaluating temporal and sequential input. In contrast to conventional RNNs, GRU uses gating mechanisms—such as update as well as reset gates—to mitigate the vanishing gradient issue and efficiently manage and maintain pertinent information over time steps. Because of this, GRU is incredibly effective and strong for jobs requiring comprehension of temporal relationships or patterns over time.

The GRU algorithm is essential for accurately and reliably diagnosing and classifying diseases in the framework of biomedical image analysis. GRU can identify intricate patterns and relationships in the data by examining the attributes that were extracted in the earlier phases of the process. These patterns and relationships may be suggestive of particular medical disorders. More accurate classifications are a result of the algorithm's capacity to concentrate on crucial sequential information, which guarantees that minute but crucial aspects in the data are successfully recorded.

The result of a multi-layered strategy that combines segmentation, feature extraction, optimization, and classification is this classification step. In biomedical pictures, segmentation identifies areas of interest, feature extraction extracts significant attributes from these areas, and optimization optimizes the system for optimal performance. Lastly, by utilizing the structured pipeline, the GRU-based categorization offers a thorough and reliable analysis. This comprehensive approach guarantees that biological image analysis is accurate, dependable, and able to support precise medical diagnosis.

Each of these steps is included in the entire process of the HBDL-FBTA framework, which is depicted in [Figure 2](#979-8-3693-9816-6.ch006.bits-pdf.xhtml#_idTextAnchor365). The proposed method, which combines innovative metaheuristic optimization with state-of-the-art deep learning algorithms, has the potential to revolutionize biomedical image processing. Its ability to deliver reliable and precise illness classification highlights its promise as a powerful tool for enhancing diagnostic accuracy and efficiency in healthcare applications.

#### Dataset

The BRATS2017 (Brain Tumor Segmentation 2017) sample serves as a prominent benchmark for the study and segmentation of brain tumors. The dataset consists of 285 MRI scans of brain tumors, each featuring four distinct MRI modalities: T1-weighted (T1), T1-weighted contrast-enhanced (T1ce), T2-weighted (T2), and Fluid Attenuated Inversion Recovery (FLAIR). These modalities offer supplementary information, facilitating a thorough analysis of cerebral tissues and neoplastic areas. Each MRI scan is accompanied by masks that delineate three essential tumor sub-regions: the Enhancing Tumor (ET), signifying the actively proliferating tumor area; the Non-Enhancing Tumor Core or Necrosis (NET/NCR), illustrating inactive or necrotic tissue; and Edema (ED), which denotes adjacent swelling or fluid accumulation. The dataset facilitates segmentation assessment across three tasks: Whole Tumor (WT), encompassing all tumor regions; Tumor Core (TC), which contains Enhancing Tumor (ET) and Non-Enhancing Tumor/Non-Critical Region (NET/NCR); and Enhancing Tumor (ET), concentrating on the active tumor region as shown in [Figure 3](#979-8-3693-9816-6.ch006.bits-pdf.xhtml#_idTextAnchor366).

Data augmentation techniques are employed to improve model performance and generalizability by artificially enlarging the dataset through the introduction of differences in the original images ([Aamir et al., 2023](#979-8-3693-9816-6.ch006.bits-pdf.xhtml#_idTextAnchor371)). Prevalent augmentation techniques encompass rotation, to simulate diverse orientations; flipping, for anatomical symmetry; scaling, to identify tumors of varying dimensions; translation, for positional discrepancies; intensity modifications, to accommodate variations in MRI acquisition parameters; and elastic deformations, which replicate natural anatomical distortions. These methods, together with the normalization of pixel intensities across modalities, provide resilient feature learning and reduce overfitting ([Aamir et al., 2022](#979-8-3693-9816-6.ch006.bits-pdf.xhtml#_idTextAnchor373)). The integration of the BRATS2017 dataset with data augmentation establishes a robust basis for training sophisticated brain tumor segmentation models, enhancing diagnosis, treatment planning, and patient outcomes.

#### Fusion-Based Extraction of Features

To extract feature vectors from the segmented images, two feature extractors are fused in this phase. In the Xception model, depthwise separable convolution took the place of separable convolution ([M. T. Aziz et. al, 2023](#979-8-3693-9816-6.ch006.bits-pdf.xhtml#_idTextAnchor377)). An “extreme” version of the Inception architecture called Xception performs better on ImageNet data than InceptionV3 and significantly outperforms it on huge datasets with 17,000 classes. Depthwise Separable convolution requires less compute than separable convolution. As a result, Xception requires less parameters than other CNN variations. The depthwise 2D convolutions used less memory and performed more slowly than standard 2D convolutions. Notably, it achieves excellent computing performance with a comparable number of model parameters as Inception. The presence or lack of nonlinearity after the initial function. By compressing and filtering input space, nonlinearity was suggested in the Inception architecture; however, Xception does not.

In this work, deep feature extraction was done using the ResNet18 version. There are eighteen layers in it. The ResNet18 architecture, which has 11,511,784 trainable parameters, was first pre-trained on the thousand classes found in the ImageNet datasets. Enabling a large number of convolutional layers is the primary goal. The network's performance deteriorates or becomes saturated because of vanishing difficulties. The network performance deteriorates when there are more layers because a vanishing gradient occurs, and the constant multiplication produces a gradient that is even smaller than the previous one. To solve the gradient vanishing problems, a novel idea known as “skip connection” was presented in this paper. By utilizing the previous layer activation, the skip connection fixes the gradient disappearing issues. By compressing the network, skip connections enable the network to learn more quickly than before.

#### Classification Based on GRU

Lastly, the classification of images is done using the GRU technique. The LSTM modules are reconstructed by the GRU network while maintaining their quality (Obayya, M et. al, 2023). The reset gate (JT) and the update gate (BT) are the two distinct gates found in every GRU cell. The GRU infrastructure is shown in [Figure 4](#979-8-3693-9816-6.ch006.bits-pdf.xhtml#_idTextAnchor367). The GRU network is used to tackle the issue of a long-dependency typical RNN network because it differs from the LSTM network.

#### GRU Framework

Following the extraction of important features from the pictures, we apply a GRU, a specialized type of neural network, to the temporal analysis of brain MRI data. GRUs are similar to an improved version of traditional Recurrent Neural Networks (RNNs), which were first proposed by Ref.42. They have the ability to identify links and patterns in data sequences. Update and reset gates are useful aspects of GRUs that aid in improved information management. We leverage the ability of a GRU with 1024 units to understand time-varying changes in brain MRI images in our design. This improves our ability to detect and categorize brain cancers. Because of its faster training and simpler architecture, the GRU outperformed other RNNs, such as LSTM, in capturing dependencies. An input gate and a forget gate are two essential parts of the LSTM type of RNN architecture. These elements are essential for controlling the network's information flow. While the forget gate chooses which information should be erased, the input gate chooses which input data is kept in the memory cell. GRUs are crucial to many Natural Language Processing (NLP) tasks, including speech recognition, machine translation, and language modeling. They are also a crucial component of our methodology, which enables the model to more accurately and effectively identify and classify brain tumors.

Courtesy:[https://medium.com/@anishnama20/understanding\-gated\-recurrent\-unit\-gru\-in\-deep\-learning\-2e54923f3e2](https://medium.com/@anishnama20/understanding-gated-recurrent-unit-gru-in-deep-learning-2e54923f3e2)

Combining the advantages of the Whale Optimization Algorithm (WOA) with Adaptive Particle Swarm Optimization (APSO), the Hybrid WOA\_APSO Algorithm is a state-of-the-art optimization method. By combining these two strategies, the algorithm improves the resilience and efficiency of the optimization process by utilizing the adaptive nature of APSO and the exploration and exploitation capabilities of WOA.

The humpback whale's bubble-net hunting technique served as the model for the Whale Optimization Algorithm (WOA). It effectively explores and exploits the search space by imitating their spiral and surrounding swimming movements. WOA uses mathematical models and control parameters like b, P, L, and m to alternate between global search (exploration) and local refining (exploitation). This equilibrium guarantees that WOA may both fine-tune solutions around the most well-known positions and diversify the search space to avoid local optima.

The conventional Particle Swarm Optimization (PSO), which is based on swarm intelligence, is improved upon by Adaptive Particle Swarm Optimization (APSO). By constantly modifying its parameters, such as acceleration coefficients and inertia weight, in response to the swarm's performance, APSO adds adaptability. This flexibility helps the algorithm avoid premature convergence and enhances the optimization process overall by balancing local refinement with global search.

These two methods are combined in the Hybrid WOA\_APSO Algorithm to produce a more reliable framework. First, the fitness of the population of search agents (particles and whales) is assessed after they are randomly initialized in the search space. The agents' positions are updated during the WOA phase in response to the encircling and spiral movements of WOA. APSO's processes are used to adaptively update particle locations and velocity during the APSO phase. The hybrid algorithm makes sure that the global best solution is refined using the best solutions from both WOA and APSO by incorporating these updates.

Until the maximum number of iterations is reached or the answer converges to an ideal value, this iterative process keeps going. In addition to improving the algorithm's capacity for exploration and exploitation, the hybridization guarantees quicker convergence by avoiding standstill. The global best position, which represents the best possible solution to the issue, is the end result. Because of its great adaptability, the Hybrid WOA\_APSO Algorithm has been used to solve a number of real-world issues, including biomedical image processing, resource allocation, feature selection, and path planning. It is an effective tool for resolving intricate optimization problems in a variety of domains because of its capacity to strike a balance between exploration and exploitation while retaining adaptability.

Hybrid WOA\_APSO Algorithm

1\. Initialize the humpback whale population Yi = (1, 2, ..., n), with i = 1.

2\. Evaluate the fitness function Fit\_ob for each Yi.

3\. while (i < maximum number of iterations) do

4\. for each search agent do

5\. Update parameters b, P, L, and m.

6\. if (m < 0.5) then

7\. if (|P| < 1) then

8\. Modify the position of the current search agent using E→=|L→⋅y→\*(ⅈ)-y→(ⅈ)|

9\. else if (|P| > 1) then

10\. Select a random search agent (Y\_random).

11\. Modify the position of the current search agent using Equation (17).

12\. Search for the minimum individual best position to determine the global best position.

13\. end if

14\. else if (m > 0.5) then

15\. Upgrade the position of the current search agent using Y(i+1).

16\. Replace the global best position using P=2b.r-b and L=2.r.

17\. end if

18\. end for

19\. Upgrade Y\* if better solution found

20\. i=i+1

21\. end while

22\. Return Y\* = best search agent

### 4\. RESULTS AND DISCUSSIONS

Confusion metrics, which divide accurate and inaccurate predictions into four different categories, were used to assess the system model's efficacy ([Figure 3](#979-8-3693-9816-6.ch006.bits-pdf.xhtml#_idTextAnchor366)):

When both the anticipated and actual results are favorable, this is known as a true positive (TP);

When a forecast indicates a positive result but the actual result is negative, this is known as a false positive (FP); When the predicted consequence and the observed outcome are both negative, this is known as a true negative (TN);while a predictor makes a mistake and predicts a negative outcome while the actual result is positive, this is known as a false negative (FN).

The accuracy, precision, recall, and F1-score are among the measures used to assess the performance of the suggested model. These metrics, such as True Positive, True Negative, False Positive, and False Negative, are computed using the information in the confusion matrix and demonstrate the model's development.

Three different metrics were used to evaluate the model's performance, and they are listed below:

The proportion of correct forecasts to all predictions is known as accuracy.

$Accuracy = ~\\frac{TP + TN}{Total~Predictions}$

The term “specificity” describes a model's innate ability to correctly locate and categorize samples that are negative within a given dataset;

$Specificity = ~\\frac{TN}{TN + FP}$

The capacity of a model to detect positive samples is known as sensitivity.

$Sensitivity = ~\\frac{TP}{TP + FN}$

This section uses brain tumor datasets from Kaggle to validate the biomedical image classifier results of the HBDL-FBTA approach. In radiology and medical imaging, these datasets are frequently utilized for the classification and study of brain tumors. The Brain Tumor Image Segmentation (BRATS) 2017 and BRATS 2020 datasets are two well-known datasets that we take into consideration for this work. As part of the Brain Tumor Segmentation Challenge, the BRATS 2017 dataset was made available with the goal of improving automated brain tumor identification using computer vision and machine learning methods. Gliomas, meningiomas, and pituitary tumors are among the various types of brain cancers that can be identified by MRI scans. To aid in precise categorization and analysis, ground truth annotations are included for every image, highlighting tumor locations and features. In a similar vein, the Brain Tumor Segmentation Competition 2020 inspired the creation of the BRATS 2020 dataset. The goal of this dataset is to enhance the identification and classification of brain cancers, specifically glioblastoma and low-grade gliomas and shown in [Figure 5](#979-8-3693-9816-6.ch006.bits-pdf.xhtml#_idTextAnchor368). It has an extensive and varied collection of MRI scans, including sequences like FLAIR, T1-weighted, and T2-weighted images. To enable thorough model evaluation, the dataset is separated into several subsets, such as training, validation, and testing sets.

In conclusion, the suggested method not only performs better than conventional and attention-enhanced models, but it also shows promise as a cutting-edge solution. Its appropriateness for real-world applications, where accuracy and dependability are crucial, is further supported by the notable accuracy enhancement.

### 5\. CONCLUSION AND FUTURE WORK

This paper introduces a unique automated biomedical image classification system called HBDL-FBTA (Hybrid Bio-inspired Deep Learning with Fusion Brain Tumor Analysis). The principal aim of the HBDL-FBTA algorithm is to proficiently evaluate biological pictures for the detection and classification of illnesses. This thorough methodology incorporates many sophisticated computational stages, guaranteeing elevated efficiency and precision in biological picture categorization.

The HBDL-FBTA approach comprises a sequence of functional phases that operate synergistically to accomplish its objectives. A pre-processing phase is utilized to improve image quality and diminish noise, which is essential for precise analysis. This is succeeded by a Swin-UNet-based segmentation technique that utilizes cutting-edge deep learning (DL) architectures to accurately delineate regions of interest in biomedical images. A fusion-based feature extraction module is employed to integrate diverse feature types, facilitating the extraction of robust and differentiated characteristics from the segmented images. A Humpback Whale Optimization with Simulated Annealing (HSSA)-based parameter tuning mechanism is subsequently employed to enhance the parameters of the classification model for improved performance. A Gated Recurrent Unit (GRU)-based classification model is employed to assess the retrieved characteristics and categorize the biological images with great reliability.

To assess the efficacy of the HBDL-FBTA system, comprehensive simulations were performed utilizing two benchmark datasets: BraTS2017, which are prominently employed in dermatological and biomedical image analysis research. The simulation results demonstrate the enhanced efficacy of the proposed HBDL-FBTA methodology in comparison to traditional deep learning methods. The model attained maximum classification accuracies of 94.51% on the ISIC 2017 dataset and 95.38% on the ISIC 2020 dataset, illustrating its capability for precise disease diagnosis. Future study and development of the HBDL-FBTA technique is promising. A crucial aspect is assessing the model's computational complexity on extensive, real-time datasets, which may yield insights into its scalability and efficiency in practical applications. Furthermore, subsequent research may investigate the amalgamation of data from several imaging modalities, including MRI, CT, and X-ray, to improve the precision and reliability of classification tasks. This multi-modal strategy possesses considerable potential for enhancing diagnosis accuracy in intricate circumstances. Furthermore, initiatives aimed at creating interpretable deep learning models, such as methods for producing saliency maps or visual elucidations, may enhance transparency, cultivate trust, and expedite the clinical integration of these automated systems in healthcare.
