## Chapter 7

# Attention-Driven Feature Fusion Synergised ViT and CNN Architectures for Brain Tumor Classification

V. Vanitha

[![Orcid Image](image/orcid-logo.png)https://orcid.org/0000-0003-1010-3241](https://orcid.org/0000-0003-1010-3241)

Sri Ramachandra Faculty of Engineering and Technology, India

Akshaya Vajpeyarr

National University of Singapore, Singapore

Arneshwar Sivakumar

[![Orcid Image](image/orcid-logo.png)https://orcid.org/0009-0001-7752-7930](https://orcid.org/0009-0001-7752-7930)

University of Edinburgh, Tiruppur, India

### ABSTRACT

Classification of brain tumors has emerged as a major issue medical diagnostics. In this research, we propose a model that integrates both CNN and Vit architectures, combined with an attention-based feature fusion mechanism to improve MRI data classification. The proposed model successfully integrates the capability of Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) in capturing localized features and that of Vision Transformers (ViTs) in capturing global contextual information. Multi-scale feature extraction is performed using DenseNet-201, followed by tokenization and embedding transformation for input into ViTs. The attention-based feature fusion enables the proposed network to dynamically integrate features at different granularities and enhance the model’s capability to classify High-Grade Gliomas (HGG), Low-Grade Gliomas (LGG), and non-tumor regions. Experimental results demonstrate superior accuracy of 97%, sensitivity, and specificity across modalities, showcasing the model's robustness and efficiency in automated brain tumor diagnosis.

### 1\. INTRODUCTION

Classifying brain tumors is vital for devising appropriate treatment plans, enhancing prognoses of patient, and enabling more targeted therapeutics. Accurately identifying tumor types is challenging due to their complex and diverse nature. Advanced imaging techniques like MRI provide detailed insights into tumor structure, location, and characteristics, forming the basis for reliable classification methods, as depicted in [Figure 1](#979-8-3693-9816-6.ch007.bits-pdf.xhtml#_idTextAnchor412).

#### Figure 1. Different tumor types with annotations: Row 1.Glioblastoma, Row 2.Lower Grade Glioma, Row 3. Meningioma, Row 4. Metastasis

![](image/979-8-3693-9816-6.ch007.f01.png)

This diversity has complicated the accurate diagnosis and treatment plan thereafter. For clinicians, it is essential to be able to differentiate among tumor types, gliomas, meningiomas, and metastatic lesions. Classification of these tumors is crucial ([Rao & Karunakara, 2021](#979-8-3693-9816-6.ch007.bits-pdf.xhtml#_idTextAnchor448)) because patient management is based on the biological behaviour, treatment protocols, and prognoses as given in Table I. However, dependence on a traditional diagnostic approach relying solely, or mostly, on the radiologist's expertise brings with it limitations that include subjective interpretation and inter-observer variability at best. Therefore, within these limits, advanced artificial intelligence techniques offer great potential.

#### Table 1. Characteristics and Treatments of Major Brain Tumor Types

| Tumor Type || Biological Behaviour || Treatment Protocols || Prognosis |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Gliomas || Originates from glial cells; can be highly invasive, often infiltrating surrounding brain tissue. || Surgery, followed by radiation and chemotherapy, depending on grade and location of the tumor. || Variable; high-grade gliomas (e.g., glioblastomas) often have poorer prognosis, while low-grade gliomas have better outcomes. |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Meningiomas || Typically, slow-growing and benign; originates from the meninges (brain and spinal cord linings). || Observation for small, asymptomatic cases; surgery for symptomatic tumors; radiation therapy if surgery is not feasible. || Generally favourable; often curable with surgery; risk of recurrence exists, especially in atypical or malignant meningiomas. |
| Metastatic Lesions || Secondary tumors that have spread from primary cancers in other organs (e.g., lung, breast). || Treatment depends on primary cancer type; includes surgery, radiation, chemotherapy, and targeted therapies. || Prognosis varies widely based on primary cancer type and stage; often associated with more advanced disease and shorter survival. |

Artificial Intelligence (AI) is revolutionizing the field of medicine. It offers immense potential to improve diagnostic accuracy, speed, and convenience across various medical specialties. AI is increasingly integrated into radiology, pathology, and other fields to aid in early disease detection staging, assessment of disease progression, and surgical planning. One of the primary benefits lies in assisting with diagnosis based on complex data, which helps healthcare professionals to identify intricate patterns that may be difficult for the human to detect ([He et al., 2023](#979-8-3693-9816-6.ch007.bits-pdf.xhtml#_idTextAnchor440)).

One significant use of AI is identifying and evaluating conditions such as cancer, cardiovascular diseases, and neurological disorders, at an initial stage. For instance, in oncology, AI algorithms are being used in the demarcation of tumours, tumour grading and in the assessment of the response to therapy ([Khan, Nasim, Ahmad, & Masood, 2024](#979-8-3693-9816-6.ch007.bits-pdf.xhtml#_idTextAnchor443)). Similarly, AI assisted image analysis has a very important role in Neurology for diseases like Alzheimer’s, Multiple sclerosis and Brain tumors. AI systems are designed to interpret MRI, Computed Tomography (CT) scans, and other such imaging modalities with very high accuracy, aiding the radiologists in identifying the areas of interest and also minimises diagnostic variability.

Although AI is currently focused on diagnosis, it holds significant potential for treatment and progress tracking. In cancer radiotherapy, accurately identifying tumor boundaries is essential to optimize treatment effectiveness and protect healthy tissue. Advanced deep learning algorithms for segmentation enhance the precision of tumor boundary detection, supporting clinicians in designing more effective treatment strategies.

#### 1.1 Challenges of AI-based Brain Tumor Classification

Classification of brain tumours using AI technology also poses several challenges due to the wide variety of tumour types, the complexity of brain anatomy, and variations in the imaging techniques. Brain tumors are categorized as primary or secondary. Secondary tumors develop from other parts of the body and spread to the brain while primary tumors originate from the brain tissue. These tumors exhibit substantial heterogeneity in appearance, size, location, and behaviour, complicating classification efforts. Early-stage tumors often resemble normal tissue, making it difficult to distinguish from healthy regions.

[Figure 2](#979-8-3693-9816-6.ch007.bits-pdf.xhtml#_idTextAnchor414) represents an organized breakdown of each primary challenge and its related factors in AI-based brain tumor classification.

#### Figure 2. Challenges in AI-based brain tumor classification

![](image/979-8-3693-9816-6.ch007.f02.png)

Classification is further complicated by the brain’s structure; with so many areas that are only slightly different from each other, making it challenging to find where the normal tissue ends and where the abnormal tissue starts, particularly in the early stages of the tumor. Further, the differences in sequences obtained from MRI also affects the development of the model because each of the sequences contains crucial information about the tumor. Some tumors, for example, need a contrast-enhanced MRI for tumor grade assessment, while others need an fMRI to understand how the tumor will affect the brain ([Zhang, Xu, Tian, Jiang, & Ma, 2021](#979-8-3693-9816-6.ch007.bits-pdf.xhtml#_idTextAnchor456)). Other barriers are as well identified by data limitations and constraints. Classification requires large annotated datasets; however, these are scarce due to the tedious and expensive process of acquiring expert labels especially in rare tumor phenotypes. This scarcity however causes AI models to be not very generalizable and introduces this possibility of bias.

Despite the advances, there are few more issues including data privacy, the problem of obtaining large and well-annotated datasets, and model interpretability ([Tang, He, Liu, & Duan, 2022](#979-8-3693-9816-6.ch007.bits-pdf.xhtml#_idTextAnchor452)). Medical imaging data is considered to be sensitive and must be handled with great care in order to comply with the data protection regulations and protect the patients’ privacy. Additionally, AI models need large volumes of well-annotated data to produce accurate results, and obtaining such data can be difficult, especially for rare conditions. Another crucial factor in developing AI is making them to be interpretable and transparent, so that health care practitioners can comprehend and trust the outcomes of these models to make correct clinical decisions.

#### 1.2 A Contemporary Research Landscape

Convolutional Neural Networks (CNN) and Vision Transformers (ViT) are two of the most critical architectural frameworks defining modern trends in computer vision and medical image analysis. Derived from natural language processing transformers, ViTs essentially re-interpret image processing; Images are segmented into patches of a predetermined size and are processed similarly to sequences of words, or embeddings. This approach enables global contextual modeling through self-attention mechanisms, allowing simultaneous consideration of relationships across entire image spaces. Like traditional CNNs, which utilise localized convolution operations to process the images, ViTs are capable of capturing long range dependencies with unprecedented efficiency that has not been observed heretofore. Hence, these novel architectures are particularly well-suited for recognizing complex patterns in medical images.

Although challenged by the transformer architectures, the CNN architecture remains primary in feature extraction and the patterning determination process. With this hierarchical design at its core, utilizing the power of convolution and pooling operations, they continue to outperform the field in recognizing the scaled patterns of local spatial hierarchies and for detecting complex features in images. In recent research, the modifications of such general CNN structures, such as dilated convolution, SE blocks, and normalization layers, have become applicable to contemporary deep learning ecosystems.

The current research direction is gradually transferring to the combined architecture of ViT and CNNs that can complement each other. Researchers are exploring fusion techniques where local feature extraction and context perception are interactive. The goal of these hybrid models is to overcome the limitations of the individual architectures, establishing more robust, flexible neural networks. Their design allows for increasingly complex visual recognition challenges in diverse domains such as medical diagnostics and perception systems.

#### 1.3 Feature Fusion: Concepts and Techniques

Feature fusion is a widely used technique that integrates data from multiple sources or representations to enhance model performance. In this context, the desired robustness and accuracy of predictions ([Kittler, Hatef, Duin, & Matas, 1998](#979-8-3693-9816-6.ch007.bits-pdf.xhtml#_idTextAnchor444)) can be improved by exploiting complementary information to construct a more informative representation. Early, late, and hybrid fusion are several types of feature fusion.

Early fusion occurs at the feature level where several features are combined before being passed to the model. In this case, the model benefits by starting its learning process from the combined data. For instance, in the medical imaging application, early fusion might involve the fusion of MRI and CT health features’ representation ([Li, Jiang, Zhang, & Zhu, 2023](#979-8-3693-9816-6.ch007.bits-pdf.xhtml#_idTextAnchor445)). Late fusion, on the other hand, occurs after models have been developed and trained on different features whereas early fusion occurs prior to the models being built. Each model provides the probability over the classes, which are combined, for instance by averaging, voting, or stacking. Late fusion enables models to specialize in various features but lacks a way of optimally utilizing all the complementary information that can be derived from the raw data ([Ahmed, Dada, & Samaila, 2023](#979-8-3693-9816-6.ch007.bits-pdf.xhtml#_idTextAnchor431)).

Early fusion and late fusion can be blended to integrate features at different stages of the modelling phase. This approach can be beneficial for complex tasks, such as classifying brain tumors, where both high- and low-level features are necessary ([Xie et al., 2022](#979-8-3693-9816-6.ch007.bits-pdf.xhtml#_idTextAnchor455); [Batool & Byun, 2024](#979-8-3693-9816-6.ch007.bits-pdf.xhtml#_idTextAnchor437)). With a strategic fusion approach, models can extract a richer set of features in more challenging domains, thus improving their prediction accuracies.

#### 1.4 Feature Fusion: Synergizing Architectural Capabilities in Medical Image Analysis

Combining both CNN and ViT using feature fusion presents a plausible solution to address the drawbacks of each in medical image analysis. CNNs are optimized for adopting the spatial organization of local details, hence useful in identifying minute details such as texture or lesion. On the other hand, ViTs are adept at modelling global dependencies by leveraging self-attention mechanisms, enabling them to understand broader contextual relationships across an image.

Patients’ medical images including MRI, CT, histopathological images that are to be diagnosed, need local cues as well as global context cues. Feature fusion of CNN and ViT architectures combines these strengths, enabling enhanced feature extraction and interpretation. It is especially useful for tasks such as multi-class tumour classification, disease localisation, and detailed anomaly detection to which the global and local nature of the images seems crucial.

Benefits of integrating CNN and ViT include increased diagnostic accuracy, enhanced generalization across different datasets and a reduced risk of overfitting in complex models. Moreover, this synergy streamlines feature hierarchies, making the models more efficient.

Key advantages of feature fusion include:

*   • Complementary Information: Different model architectures excel at capturing different types of information. CNNs effectively extract local spatial features while ViTs model long-range dependencies well. These complementary features enable a more complete interpretation of input data.
    
*   • Reduced Overfitting: Feature fusion can reduce the likelihood of overfitting, which is an issue that often arises when using deep learning algorithms. By incorporating features learned from all these combined sources, the model becomes more robust to variability and noise.
    
*   • Enhanced Performance: Feature fusion improves the performance of deep learning algorithms consistently. Models can achieve higher accuracy, sensitivity and specificity results by using strengths of various architectures.
    
*   • Improved Interpretability: It can also enhance interpretability of deep learning models. Through visualization of the fused features, one can better understand how the model has arrived at the decision, and which aspects played a crucial role in leading the final prediction.
    

### 2\. LITERATURE REVIEW

Brain tumor classification has gained significant attention in recent years, driven by advancements in deep learning techniques. Several approaches, including CNNs, transfer learning, Vision Transformers, and hybrid models, have been analysed in this section.

[Aamir et al. (2022)](#979-8-3693-9816-6.ch007.bits-pdf.xhtml#_idTextAnchor430) proposed a multiscale CNN framework along with data augmentation and sliding window testing to reduce bias and prevent overfitting. [Khan et al. (2020)](#979-8-3693-9816-6.ch007.bits-pdf.xhtml#_idTextAnchor442) developed an automated MM-Brain Tumor classifier utilizing deep learning, where VGG16 and VGG19 architectures were employed for precise feature selection. Contrast stretching was applied to enhance tumor visibility, and feature selection was conducted to reduce computational load. However, the study encountered several challenges, including the high similarity in tumor structures of certain types, the impact of low contrast in T1-weighted images on feature extraction, and the inherent complexities of multimodal classification.

[Mohsen et al. (2017)](#979-8-3693-9816-6.ch007.bits-pdf.xhtml#_idTextAnchor447) utilized CNN, discrete wavelet transform (DWT) for feature extraction and principal component analysis (PCA) for dimensionality reduction, classifying MRIs into four broad categories. Their approach achieved classification accuracy comparable to traditional CNNs, with less equipment and faster computation. However, the study's limitations include the small dataset size and reliance on T2-weighted images, restricting its broader application.

[Ari and Hanbay (2018)](#979-8-3693-9816-6.ch007.bits-pdf.xhtml#_idTextAnchor434) proposed an Extreme Learning Machine with Local Receptive Fields (ELM-LRF) for classifying MR images as benign or malignant. The main limitation is the small dataset, consisting of images from only 16 patients. In [Srinivas et al. (2022)](#979-8-3693-9816-6.ch007.bits-pdf.xhtml#_idTextAnchor450), authors discussed the use of deep transfer learning techniques in classifying brain tumours based on MR images. VGG-16 yielded the best performance results after intensity normalization and re-sizing preprocessing the data. [Badjie and Ülker (2022)](#979-8-3693-9816-6.ch007.bits-pdf.xhtml#_idTextAnchor436) developed a deep learning-based architecture that leverages pre-trained networks, fine-tuning them for tumor classification to effectively detect and differentiate various tumor types in MRI scans.

[Mehrotra et al. (2020)](#979-8-3693-9816-6.ch007.bits-pdf.xhtml#_idTextAnchor446) evaluated various models including AlexNet, GoogLeNet, ResNet 50, ResNet 101, and SqueezeNet. However, they used only 696 MRI image samples which may not generalize well especially in large scale applications. Hao et al (18) introduced an innovative active learning framework leveraging transfer learning to minimize annotation costs. The performance yields an AUC of 82.89% on the test dataset and with augmentation all labelling costs are reduced by 40% mark.

[Ali (2023)](#979-8-3693-9816-6.ch007.bits-pdf.xhtml#_idTextAnchor432) introduced ViT-BT, a Vision Transformer-based model designed for brain tumor classification. The ViT-BT framework enhances classification performance by first pre-training the Vision Transformer model and then fine-tuning it using specialized MRI brain tumor datasets with an accuracy of 98%. [Reddy et al. (2024)](#979-8-3693-9816-6.ch007.bits-pdf.xhtml#_idTextAnchor449) implemented a variant of vision transformer for automatically classifying multiple classes of brain tumor from the MRI scan images. Several pre-trained models were compared in the study, with the FTVT-l16 model performing best with a test accuracy of 98.70%.

[Tummala et al. (2022)](#979-8-3693-9816-6.ch007.bits-pdf.xhtml#_idTextAnchor453) proposed an ensemble of ViT models for tumor classification. Pretrained ViT models on ImageNet were fine-tuned and utilized for the classification task. The proposed model achieved an accuracy of 98.7%. [Goceri (2023)](#979-8-3693-9816-6.ch007.bits-pdf.xhtml#_idTextAnchor439) leveraged advantages of CNN and ViT to develop a novel architecture for glioma classification through the effective integration of feature-combining modules. Experimental results demonstrated the approach's efficacy in classifying four glioma subtypes from histopathological images, achieving an accuracy of 96.75%.

[Karagoz et al. (2024)](#979-8-3693-9816-6.ch007.bits-pdf.xhtml#_idTextAnchor441) introduced a self-supervised technique to address the issue of limited availability in datasets. The dual CNN & Vision Transformer approach is pre-trained and fine-tuned. Synthetic MRI imagery is used to balance datasets by augmenting them, thereby increasing classification efficiency and reducing overfitting. This model demonstrated excellent performance as well as generalization capability to other databases but the usage of fake images indicates that there may be some biases inherent to the generated synthetic images.

[Asiri et al. (2023)](#979-8-3693-9816-6.ch007.bits-pdf.xhtml#_idTextAnchor435) introduced the FT-ViT model, a fine-tuned Vision Transformer leveraging image processing and deep learning techniques to classify tumors. The framework comprises multiple stages, including data preprocessing, patch extraction, feature concatenation, selection, learning, and fine-tuning. Trained on the CE-MRI dataset, which includes 5,712 brain tumor images, the FT-ViT achieved 98.13% accuracy. DeepTumorNet ([Asiri et al., 2023](#979-8-3693-9816-6.ch007.bits-pdf.xhtml#_idTextAnchor435)) is a hybrid deep learning model designed for brain tumor classification. The architecture integrates a modified GoogLeNet with leaky ReLU activation. The results demonstrated that the model outperformed comparable methods, achieving an accuracy of 99.67% and a recall of 100%.

[Vimala et al. (2023)](#979-8-3693-9816-6.ch007.bits-pdf.xhtml#_idTextAnchor454) utilized EfficientNets to classify brain tumors using the Figshare dataset. EfficientNetB2, fine-tuned with additional layers and Grad-CAM visualization for interpretability, outperformed other models. [Dixon et al (2024)](#979-8-3693-9816-6.ch007.bits-pdf.xhtml#_idTextAnchor438) proposed a hybrid architecture combining ViT and CNNs for robust brain tumor classification. The framework integrates texture, structural, and deep features, leveraging Haralick features, local binary patterns, and ViT-derived features. Evaluations demonstrate superior performance on diverse brain MRI datasets. [Aloraini et al. (2023)](#979-8-3693-9816-6.ch007.bits-pdf.xhtml#_idTextAnchor433) proposed a hybrid model for brain tumor classification, combining CNNs for local feature extraction and transformers for global feature attention. The model achieves average accuracies of 96.75% on the BraTS 2018 dataset and 99.10% on the Figshare dataset. [Tabatabaei et al. (2023)](#979-8-3693-9816-6.ch007.bits-pdf.xhtml#_idTextAnchor451) proposed a two-branch parallel model combining a Transformer Module (TM), and CNN for brain tumor classification. Using a cross-fusion strategy, local and global features are integrated to enhance accuracy. The lightweight iResNet architecture outperformed other CNN variants, achieving 99.30% accuracy.

As indicated in the literature review, there are improvements for classification of brain tumours (Verma et al., 2023; Garg et al., 2024), however the studies present several issues that restricts the effectiveness for broader uses. One common issue identified is the limited or unbalanced datasets, as cited in [Ari and Hanbay’s (2018)](#979-8-3693-9816-6.ch007.bits-pdf.xhtml#_idTextAnchor434) and a similar case in [Mehrotra et al (2020)](#979-8-3693-9816-6.ch007.bits-pdf.xhtml#_idTextAnchor446). These limitations impair transferability and reliability of the models, particularly within the clinical practice where numerous patient groups and imaging modalities are used. Further, the inclusion of synthetic data for augmentation as done in [Karagoz, Nalbantoglu, & Fox (2024)](#979-8-3693-9816-6.ch007.bits-pdf.xhtml#_idTextAnchor441) pose some biases. Though synthetic data is beneficial since it can minimize the impact of small dataset; however, it will not always reflect real-world situations, thus the model’s efficiency declines when tested on other datasets.

There are also major issues regarding the computational and training issues. Approaches by ([Reddy et al., 2024](#979-8-3693-9816-6.ch007.bits-pdf.xhtml#_idTextAnchor449); [Tummala et al., 2022](#979-8-3693-9816-6.ch007.bits-pdf.xhtml#_idTextAnchor453)) need substantial computational resources for pretraining and fine-tuning, so they are not practically viable in resource constrained settings. In addition, many hybrid models such as DeepTumorNet ([Asiri et al., 2023](#979-8-3693-9816-6.ch007.bits-pdf.xhtml#_idTextAnchor435)) are prone to overfitting due to the highly fine-tuned parameters and a limited amount of data. This may decrease the model’s ability to generalize to the other datasets or other clinical applications.

The literature highlights some of the major difficulties in feature extraction, which have a direct relationship on the performance as well as the efficacy of the models used in brain tumor classification. One of the major challenges is that the structures of different types of tumors do not vary significantly, which poses a challenge to the models to discern in between them well. Additionally, low contrast in T1-weighted images poses a significant obstacle, as it hampers the extraction of meaningful features necessary for accurate classification. Multimodal classification is also inherently difficult because information derived from the various imaging modalities has to be combined and interpreted by the model. The aforementioned challenges imply that misclassifications are more likely to happen when the models are used in real clinical practice. This underscores the need to develop sophisticated feature extraction methods and reliable data fusion approaches.

The work shows the potential and limitations of Transfer Learning (TF), Vision Transformers (ViT), and ViT-CNN integrated models in brain tumour classification. TF models, often starting from VGG16 or ResNet, work well with feature extraction but fail at identifying tumor features when the size of the set of images is relatively small or unbalanced. It has been found that the use of ViTs is appropriate of large amounts of data and gets high accuracy but consumes a lot of computational power and does not capture local details. The ViT-CNN hybrids have better performance than the ViT and CNN approaches; however, they are complicated and may overfit on small datasets.

### 3\. REVIEW OF APPROACHES IMPLEMENTED IN BRAIN TUMOR CLASSIFICATION

#### 3.1 DenseNet-210

For the proposed hybrid model, DenseNet-201 serves as the primary CNN architecture. [Figure 3](#979-8-3693-9816-6.ch007.bits-pdf.xhtml#_idTextAnchor415) illustrates the detailed structure of DenseNet-20. The most distinctive feature of DenseNet-201 is connectivity, which implies the concatenation of the previous layer’s features with all the subsequent layers. This connectivity structure enhances the flow of information which makes DenseNet-201 appropriate for extracting complex features in different applications. Let x[0] represent the input to the network, and f[1],f[2],f[3],…f[l-1],f[L] denote the output from each of the L layers in the dense block. The input to layer l is the combined output from the earlier layers:

f[l]\=H(\[x[0,] f[1],f[2],f[3],…f[l-1]\]) (1)

where H(⋅) represents the composite function applied in layer l, which typically includes operations like Batch Normalization, ReLU activation, and convolution.

#### Figure 3. Architecture of DenseNet-201

![](image/979-8-3693-9816-6.ch007.f03.png)

The structure of DenseNet is made of dense block and transition layers. A dense block has many convolutional layers, and each layer is connected with all other layers through dense connectivity. In this case there are transition layers between the dense blocks which assist in down sampling the feature maps using average pooling. Additionally, the growth rate, which determines the number of new features added by each layer, is kept relatively low to ensure computational efficiency while preserving model performance.

The output of DenseNet-201 features is passed through a Multilayer Perceptron with two fully connected layers, each containing 512 neurons each. These layers are interspersed with BN (Batch Normalization) to increase the stability of the learning process. Leaky ReLU is used as the activation function, defined as:

  
$$f\\left( z \\right) = \\left\\{ \\begin{matrix} {z~z > 0} \\\\ {\\alpha z~z \\leq 0} \\\\ \\end{matrix}\\operatorname{} \\right.$$  
(2)

where α prevents dead neurons and is constant, allowing neurons to handle negative inputs.

#### 3.2 Vision Transformer

The Vision Transformer represents a shift from conventional paradigms in computer vision to the currently popular Transformer models in natural language processing. In 2020, researchers at Google Brain developed ViT, applying the self-attention mechanism of Transformers to image data, in contrast to the standard sequence data used in NLP. This approach addresses the limitations of CNN such as restricted global context awareness. Thus, ViT became a notable architecture, particularly in large-scale image classification, achieving significant results and marking a new era in research.

ViT differs fundamentally from CNNs in the way it processes images. Traditional CNNs work hierarchically by extracting more and more abstract features from the localized receptive field to understand the image content. In contrast, ViT treats images as a sequence of fixed-sized grids. This is similar to how NLP models treat sentences as sequences of words. In this innovative approach, the input image is segmented into image patches. Each of them is linearly transformed into a one-dimensional vector through a learnable embedding layer. These embedded patches effectively act as tokens to be processed by Transformer models similar to word tokens in NLP.

The key component of ViT as shown in [figure 4](#979-8-3693-9816-6.ch007.bits-pdf.xhtml#_idTextAnchor416) is the encoder which forms the backbone of the model. Each block contains a self-attention mechanism and then a feedforward neural network with the addition of residual connections and layer normalization. The self-attention mechanism evaluates the dependencies of the patches adaptively, focusing on the critical regions of the image. This enable ViT to learn long-range contexts and capture global information, while avoiding the need for many parameters, as is the case of traditional CNNs’ convolutional kernels.

#### Figure 4. Architecture of Vision Transformer

![](image/979-8-3693-9816-6.ch007.f04.png)

To preserve the spatial structure of the image, ViT adds learnable positional embeddings on the patch embeddings. This is because the Transformer models are naturally order-agnostic by default and do not inherently understand token layout. The model keeps the spatial structure by using positional embeddings to know the position of every patch in the image. When combined with the self-attention mechanism, these embeddings make ViT learn to capture the local and the global spatial structures, and thus perform even better in learning spatial patterns.

This concept, originally introduced in the BERT model for NLP tasks, serves as a global representation of the entire image in ViT. As the image is processed, the CLS token interacts with all other patches via the self-attention mechanism, collecting features that represent the overall content of the image. Once the image passes through the final Transformer encoder layer, the CLS token is passed through a linear classification layer, where it is used to generate the model's final prediction. By incorporating both local and global features, this approach enables ViT to effectively analyse and classify images.

The computational power and the large datasets deemed necessary for training ViT models effectively are substantial. Unlike CNNs that have certain built-in biases such as spatial hierarchies and local patterns (e.g., edges and textures), ViT is not affected by these inherent biases. For this reason, ViT models require pretraining on large datasets such as ImageNet-21k or JFT-300M to learn high quality representations. Then they can be fine-tuned using task specific datasets to perform well. This pretraining-finetuning approach of ViT enables it to generalize better and often outperforms CNN models in large-scale classification tasks.

Despite these advantages, the computational complexity of ViT is a big issue. However, the self-attention mechanism is highly resource intensive, scaling quadratically with the number of patches, which is especially significant given that ViTs work well with high-resolution images. The model needs to compute all patch interactions, resulting in quadratic memory and processing power scaling. However, while these high demands are required for ViT in resource limited settings they can be impractical. In order to address these challenges, researchers have developed solutions including sparse self-attention as well as these hierarchical Transformer architectures, which come at a reduced computational cost but maintain strong performance.

The rise in popularity of Vision Transformers has led to the development of various hybrid architectures that merge advantages from both fields of CNNs and transformers. Models like the Swin transformer and DeiT (Data-efficient Image Transformers) combine the power of local feature extraction achieved through the CNN structure with the global context-awareness of transformers. Conventional models provide a regional fit, making hybrid models appropriate for small datasets. For instance, Swin transformer models utilize hierarchical structuring to process images at varying resolutions to make it far less computationally expensive without compromising accuracy. These improvements help address the limitations of ViT and make these models more practical for real-world use.

### 4\. PROPOSED METHODOLOGY

This work proposes a hybrid architecture with a novel attention-based feature fusion mechanism to classify the MRI of the BRaTS dataset into three categories.

The contributions of this work are:

1.  1\. Novel Hybrid Architecture: A hybrid framework that integrates the advantages of CNN and ViT is proposed. It aims to capture and integrate both global and local information from images.
    
2.  2\. Attention driven Feature Fusion Module: A novel feature fusion mechanism is proposed that combines features at various granularities using a cross-attention mechanism. This allows the module to seamlessly integrate global contextual patterns with localized details through the cross-attention mechanism. This dynamic fusion process also adjusts the importance of features while simultaneously increasing the variety of captured information, without merely including other features.
    

The proposed method consists of three interconnected components as shown in [figure 5](#979-8-3693-9816-6.ch007.bits-pdf.xhtml#_idTextAnchor417).

#### Figure 5. Hybrid CNN-ViT architecture with attention-based feature fusion mechanism

![](image/979-8-3693-9816-6.ch007.f05.png)

1.  1\. CNN\-Based Multi\-Scale Feature Extraction:
    

This component employs DenseNet-201 to generate feature maps at three distinct spatial scales: features at the coarse level (global structural patterns), medium level (intermediate anatomical details), and fine level (localized and textural information). The module produces detailed and diverse representations by extracting features across multiple scales.

1.  2\. ViT Feature Refinement:
    

The attention mechanism in these transformers enhances CNN-derived features with contextual information, resulting in structured and high-quality feature map representations.

1.  3\. Cross\-Attention Feature Fusion Model:
    

This mechanism enables interaction between feature maps of different scales from the three ViTs, optimizing the feature maps with refinements and consolidating the integrated results into a single feature map. The cross-attention mechanism uses the information from the coarse, medium, and fine feature levels to yield a unified multi scale representation tailored to be used in classification.

The following section will detail each component of the architecture, elucidating its architecture and function in the overall system.

#### 4.1 CNN-Based Multi-Scale Feature Extraction

DenseNet-201 is designed to have dense connectivity across its layers. This structure enhances the flow of gradients during backpropagation and improves feature reuse. The model is organized into several dense blocks, with each block extracting features at different levels of abstraction. For brain tumor classification, we aim to extract fine, medium, and coarse features from these blocks to capture various spatial patterns and structures in brain images.

The reasons for choosing DenseNet-201 as the CNN Component are as follows:

Dense Connectivity: Within each dense block, every layer utilizes feature maps from all preceding layers, enabling an efficient mechanism for feature reuse. This approach captures subtle and nuanced features, which are crucial for precise diagnosis.

Feature Preservation: Unlike traditional CNNs which suffer from feature loss, DenseNet-201 maintains and combines features from earlier layers throughout the network. This characteristic is crucial in medical imaging, where early-stage feature details can be as important as high-level semantic features. The dense connectivity allows for comprehensive feature preservation and aggregation.

Parameter Efficiency: Despite its depth (201 layers), DenseNet-201 achieves remarkable parameter efficiency. The dense connectivity pattern reduces the need for redundant feature maps, resulting in a more compact model. This is particularly beneficial for medical image classification, where model complexity and computational requirements must be balanced with precision.

Multi\-Scale Feature Extraction: DenseNet-201's architecture naturally supports multi-scale feature extraction. The dense blocks capture features at different levels of abstraction, ranging from low-level texture details to high-level semantic representations. This multi-scale approach is ideal for medical image analysis, where tumors and pathological conditions can manifest in various subtle ways.

DenseNet-201, with its dense connections, parameter efficiency, and multi-scale feature extraction capabilities, provides high-quality hierarchical feature maps that are ideal for a hybrid CNN-ViT architecture. When combined with the Vision Transformer’s long-range dependency modeling, this setup leverages the strengths of both paradigms, making it highly effective for challenging tasks like brain tumor classification.

Extraction of Fine Features (Dense Block 1)

Dense block 1 is responsible for extracting fine features, which includes low-level details and small anatomical structures. The input image, denoted as X[0], passes through the initial convolution layer before being processed by the dense block layers. Each convolution operation within this block takes the output from all previous layers, enabling the model to capture increasingly complex patterns. Mathematically, the output of the i^(th) convolutional layer within Dense Block 1 is represented as:

Y[i]\=σ(W[i]∗X[i]−1+b[i]) (3)

where W[i] is the convolution kernel, b[i] is the bias term, ∗ denotes the convolution operation, and σ is the non-linear activation function (ReLU). After processing through all layers in Dense Block 1, the output feature map, denoted as F[fine], represents the fine-grained details.

Extraction of Medium Features (Dense Block 2)

After extracting fine features from Dense Block 1, the next step is to capture medium features. These features are abstracted from the fine-level details and represent intermediate anatomical patterns, such as larger structures or patterns within the brain. The output from Dense Block 1, denoted as F[fine] , is passed to Dense Block 2, where additional layers further process the features. The mathematical representation of this transition from Dense Block 1 to Dense Block 2 is as follows:

F[medium]\=f[block](F[fine]) (4)

where f[block] refers to the operations performed within Dense Block 2, including additional convolutional layers and batch normalization. The resulting output F[medium] contains medium-level features, which abstract away finer details and begin to capture larger anatomical structures. These medium features are essential for identifying intermediate tumor characteristics and structures that span across smaller regions in the image. Additionally, these features can also help detect relationships between different brain regions which are essential for accurate tumor diagnosis.

Extraction of Coarse Features (Dense Block 3)

Dense Block 3 captures the coarse features, which represent the highest level of abstraction in the feature extraction process. These coarse features are global, large-scale patterns that encompass significant structures, such as the entire tumor or other broader brain regions. The output from Dense Block 2, denoted as F[medium] is passed to Dense Block 3 for further processing. The mathematical transition from Dense Block 2 to Dense Block 3 is represented as:

F[coarse]\=f[block](F[medium]) (5)

where f[block] represents the operations within Dense Block 3, including further convolutions and batch normalization. The resulting output F[coarse] contains coarse features, which are abstracted and provide a global understanding of the brain's structures. These coarse features are essential for recognizing the overall tumor region, its size, and its relationship with other parts of the brain. The coarse features provide the model with context about the tumor's location within the brain, which is critical for making final classification decisions.

Table II summarizes the dimensions of output at different stages of the DenseNet-201 architecture for an input size of 240×240×4. After the first convolution layer and pooling layer, the spatial dimensions are halved. Output size after initial convolution and pooling is 120×120×64 where 64 is the number of filters/channels. This serves as input to the first dense block.

#### Table 2. Dimensions of feature maps at various stages of DenseNet-201

| Stage || Spatial Size || Channels |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Initial Input || 120×120 || 64 |
| --- | --- | --- |
| After Dense Block 1 || 120×120 || 92 |
| After Transition 1 || 60×60 || 128 |
| After Dense Block 2 || 60×60 || 384 |
| After Transition 2 || 30×30 || 256 |

#### 4.2 ViT Feature Refinement

The integration of Convolutional Neural Network with Vision Transformer represents a critical computational challenge in modern computer vision architectures. This transformation requires a sophisticated approach to convert hierarchical feature maps into a tokenized format compatible with transformer-based models. This section proposes a systematic approach for such transformation, with a focus on handling features at multiple granularities to enable hierarchical representation learning.

##### 4.2.1 Mathematical Formulation of Feature Map Transformation

Let the CNN-extracted feature map at granularity level g {fine, medium, coarse} be denoted as be F[g] , represented mathematically as:

  
*F*[*g*] ∈ *R*^(*w*[*g* × *H*[*g*]  × *c*[*g*] ])   
(6)

where H represents the height, W the width, and C the number of channels of the feature map. ViTs require tokenized inputs, where each token corresponds to a fixed-length vector. This necessitates:

1.  1\. Flattening of spatial dimensions height (H[g]) and width (W[g]) into a single dimension.
    
2.  2\. Projection of the resulting tokens into an embedding space of dimension d, which aligns with the ViT input specifications.
    

##### 4.2.2 Tokenization and Embedding Transformation

Tokenization and embedding transformation are critical steps that adapt image data into a format suitable for processing by transformer architectures. The steps involved in this process is detailed below.

###### 4.2.2.1 Flattening CNN Feature Maps.

The spatial dimensions H[g]×W[g] are flattened, converting the feature map F[g] into a matrix *F*[*g*]^(*f**l**a**t*) as:

*F*[*g*] ∈ *R*^(*w*[*g* × *H*[*g*]  × *c*[*g*] ])  (7)

For a feature map F[g]∈R^(64×16×16F),flattening produces F[g]^(flat)∈R^(256×64) (i.e., 256 tokens, each of dimension 64).

###### 4.2.2.2 Linear Projection to Embedding Space.

Flattened feature map F[g]^(flat) is projected into a lower-dimensional space using a learnable linear projection matrix *W*[*g*]^(*p**r**o**j*) and the bias term *b*[*g*]^(*p**r**o**j*)as given in (8)

E[g]\=   
*F*[*g*]^(*f**l**a**t*)  
⋅  
*W*[*g*]^(*p**r**o**j*)  
+  
*b*[*g*]^(*p**r**o**j*)  
(8)

Where *W*[*g*]^(*p**r**o**j*)∈ R^(Cg×d): Linear projection matrix that reduces C[g]\-dimensional tokens to d- dimensional embeddings. *b*[*g*]^(*p**r**o**j*)∈R^d:Bias term added to each token embedding.

The resulting token embeddings E[g] are given by:

  
*E*[*g* ] ∈ *R*^((*H*[*g*.]*W*[*g*)*X**d*])   
(9)

###### 4.2.2.3 Processing Tokenized Features with Vision Transformers.

The tokenized embeddings *E*[*g* ] are processed through a dedicated ViT block for each granularity level g:

  
*F*[*g* ]^′ = *V**i**T**B**l**o**c**k*(*E*[*g* ])  
(10)

where *F*[*g* ]^′′ represents the refined features. Each ViT block consists of:

*   • Multi-head self-attention (MHSA) layers for capturing long-range dependencies.
    
*   • Feedforward layers for non-linear transformations.
    

The independent processing of *E*[*g* ] at different granularities enables the model to extract multi-scale representations critical for downstream tasks.

#### 4.3 Cross-Attention Feature Fusion Model

The proposed fusion technique addresses the challenge of effectively integrating multi-granularity feature representations. The model begins with three distinct feature maps extracted from different levels of granularity as shown in [figure 6](#979-8-3693-9816-6.ch007.bits-pdf.xhtml#_idTextAnchor419).

#### Figure 6. Multi Scale Feature Extraction using DenseNet-201

![](image/979-8-3693-9816-6.ch007.f06.png)

Let *F*[1 ]^′, *F*[2 ]^′, *F*[3 ]^′ represent feature maps extracted from coarse-, mid-, and fine-level ViTs, respectively. These feature maps, obtained after tokenization and embedding transformation, are of varying spatial resolutions and semantic granularity. To enable effective fusion, all feature maps are projected into a common feature dimension d:

  
*F*[*i*]^′  
\=   
$$W\_{i}F\_{i~} + ~b\_{\\begin{matrix} {i~} \\\\ ~ \\\\ ~ \\\\ \\end{matrix}}~$$  
(11)

*W*[*i*] ∈ *R*^(*d**X**d*^′) where *W*[*i*] *a**n**d* *b*[*i* ]are learnable projection parameters, and d′ is the original feature dimension.

##### 4.3.1 Cross-Attention Blocks

To fuse information, three cross-attention blocks are defined, where each feature map alternates as the query while the remaining two serve as keys and values. The Cross-attention Feature fusion is depicted in [figure 7](#979-8-3693-9816-6.ch007.bits-pdf.xhtml#_idTextAnchor420).

#### Figure 7. Cross-Attention Feature Fusion

![](image/979-8-3693-9816-6.ch007.f07.png)

Block 1: Coarse-level features *F*[1]^′ as query.

Q[1]\=*F*[1]^′W[Q], K[2]\=*F*[2]^′W[K], V[2]\=*F*[2]^′W[V], K3= *F*[3]^′W[K], V[3]\=*F*[3]^′W[V]

where W[Q] W[k], W[v] ∈R^(d×d′) are learnable projection matrices for queries, keys, and values. The cross-attention output is computed as:

  
 *F*[1]^(*o**u**t*)  
\=   
$$Softmax\\left( \\frac{Q\_{1}K\_{2}^{T}}{\\sqrt{d^{'}}} \\right.$$  
)  
$$~V\_{2~} + ~Softmax\\left( \\frac{Q\_{1}K\_{3}^{T}}{\\sqrt{d^{'}}} \\right.$$  
)  
 *V*[3 ]   
(12)

Block 2: Mid-level features *F*[2]^′ as query.

Q[2]\=*F*[2]^′W[Q], K[1]\=*F*[1]^′W[K], V[1]\=*F*[1]^′W[V], K[3]\= *F*[3]^′W[K], V[3]\=*F*[3]^′W[V]

  
*F*[2]^(*o**u**t*)  
\=   
$$Softmax\\left( \\frac{Q\_{2}K\_{1}^{T}}{\\sqrt{d^{'}}} \\right.$$  
)  
$$~V\_{1~} + ~Softmax\\left( \\frac{Q\_{2}K\_{3}^{T}}{\\sqrt{d^{'}}} \\right.$$  
)  
 *V*[3 ]  
(13)

Block 3: Fine-level features *F*[3]^′ as query.

Q[3]\=*F*[3]^′W[Q], K[1]\=*F*[1]^′W[K], V[1]\=*F*[1]^′W[V], K[2]\= *F*[2]^′W[K], V[3]\=*F*[2]^′W[V]

  
 *F*[3]^(*o**u**t*)  
\=   
$$Softmax\\left( \\frac{Q\_{3}K\_{1}^{T}}{\\sqrt{d^{'}}} \\right.$$  
)  
$$~V\_{1~} + ~Softmax\\left( \\frac{Q\_{3}K\_{2}^{T}}{\\sqrt{d^{'}}} \\right.$$  
)  
 *V*[2 ]  
(14)

##### 4.3.2 Residual Connections and Normalization

Residual connections and layer normalization are applied to each cross-attention output to stabilize training and enhance feature representation,

  
*F*[*i*]^(*r**e**s*)  
\= LayerNorm (  
*F*[*i*]^′+ *F*[*i*]^(*o**u**t*))  
(15)

##### 4.3.3 Concatenation and Fully Connected Fusion

The residual outputs from all three blocks are concatenated:

  
*F*[*c**o**n**c**a**t*] = *C**o**n**c**a**t*\[*F*[1]^(*r**e**s*) ,*F*[2]^(*r**e**s*) ,*F*[3]^(*r**e**s*)\]  
(16)

The concatenated features are then passed through a multi-layer perceptron to generate the final fused feature representation:

  
*F*[*f**u**s**e**d*] = *M**L**P*(*F*[*c**o**n**c**a**t*])  
(17)

Algorithm: Attention Based Feature Fusion

Inputs:

*   • *F*[1 ]^′, *F*[2 ]^′, *F*[3 ]^′ : Feature maps from ViTs at coarse, mid, and fine granular levels, with sizes B×N ×d[1], B×N[2]×d[2], B×N[3]×d[3].
    
*   • d′: Common feature dimension for fusion.
    

Output:*F*[*f**u**s**e**d*]: Fused feature map.

### 5\. EXPERIMENTAL SETUP AND RESULT

#### 5.1 Experimental Setup

Models were implemented using Python-based libraries and executed on a desktop equipped with a CPU-Intel Core i9-13900K CPU alongside a GPU - NVIDIA GeForce RTX 3090. A deep learning-based classification framework was developed for analyzing MRI using convolutional neural networks (CNNs). The framework performed multiclass classification to categorize tumors into four distinct types. The implementation utilized Python-based deep learning libraries, specifically Keras with TensorFlow backend, within the Anaconda environment.

#### 5.2 Dataset

The BraTS 2015 (Brain Tumor Segmentation) dataset represents a significant milestone in medical imaging resources, comprising multimodal MRI scans from 220 high-grade glioma (HGG) cases and 54 low-grade glioma (LGG) cases. Each case in the dataset contains four distinct MRI sequences: T1-weighted (T1), T1-weighted with contrast enhancement (T1ce), T2-weighted (T2), and Fluid Attenuated Inversion Recovery (FLAIR).

Rigorous preprocessing was undertaken on the dataset to ensure standardization across all cases of the dataset. All images were manually annotated by expert neuroradiologists. A key feature of the BraTS 2015 dataset is the inclusion of detailed segmentation masks and classification labels. Tumor regions were annotated using a hierarchical segmentation approach: label 1 for necrosis, non-enhancing tumor, and cyst; label 2 for edema; label 4 for enhancing tumor; and label 0 for all other areas. These annotations serve as a benchmark for developing and testing of automated segmentation algorithms. The unique advantage of the BraTS 2015 dataset lies in the inclusion of both HGG and LGG cases, making it invaluable for creating classification and segmentation algorithms that are both effective and robust.

Samples of the four MRI modalities are illustrated in [Figure 8](#979-8-3693-9816-6.ch007.bits-pdf.xhtml#_idTextAnchor421). Each modality includes 155 slices, resulting in 620 images per case. For the 274 cases, this results in a total of 169,880 MRI images, as detailed in Table III. The dataset is divided into 80% for training and 20% for testing. For this study, we categorized the dataset into three classes:

*   • Class 1 represents High-Grade Gliomas (HGG) and includes Necrosis (1), Enhancing Tumor (4), and extensive Edema (2), as these features indicate aggressive tumor behaviour.
    
*   • Class 2 represents Low-Grade Gliomas (LGG) and includes images labelled as Non-enhancing Tumor (3).
    
*   • Finally, Class 0, labelled as non-tumor.

##### 5.3.4 Loss-Accuracy Curve and Confusion Matrix Analysis

[Figure 12](#979-8-3693-9816-6.ch007.bits-pdf.xhtml#_idTextAnchor428) illustrates the accuracy and loss curves for DenseNet201, Vision Transformer (ViT), and the proposed model. For DenseNet201 the accuracy steadily increases but at a slow rate, stagnating around 0.85. The pattern observed in training accuracy and the validation accuracy graph suggests overfitting. While the training loss sharply decreases and converges to a very low value, the validation loss reduces more slowly, indicating minor generalization issues. The training and validation accuracy of ViT shows a gradual progress through epochs and stabilises at approximately 0.9. However, there is still a small gap between the training and validation accuracy, indicating potential overfitting. On the other hand, the proposed hybrid model achieves high accuracy (0.97) early in training, with both training and validation losses converging quickly to nearly zero. This suggests better efficiency and reduced overfitting in comparison to the baseline models, highlighting the proposed model's superiority over existing alternatives.

#### Figure 12. Training and Validation Accuracy - Loss plots for three models.10

![](image/979-8-3693-9816-6.ch007.f12.png)

The normalized confusion matrix is shown in [figure 13](#979-8-3693-9816-6.ch007.bits-pdf.xhtml#_idTextAnchor429).

#### Figure 13. Normalised Confusion matrix for the proposed model

![](image/979-8-3693-9816-6.ch007.f13.png)

The proposed model provides a great classification of HGG with true positive rate of 0.98. However, a very small proportion of the HGG samples is misclassified to LGG (0.01) and Nontumor (0.01) also. This suggests that although the model is efficient in detecting aggressive results for tumor morphology, there might be some overlap of distinct features with LGG and Nontumor, which may be tuned or refined further in the future. As with LGG, the true positive rate of the model is 0.97 and reflects the ability of the model to effectively segment low-grade glioma areas. However, 0.02% of LGG samples are misclassified as HGG probably because the tumor characteristics of the two grades may be quite similar. Furthermore, it is detected that 0.01 of LGG samples are misclassified as Nontumor, which might stem from feature similarity or noise of input data. For Nontumor, the model achieves a true positive rate of 0.98, showcasing its ability to accurately detect non-tumor regions. A minimal proportion of these samples is misclassified as HGG (0.01) or LGG (0.01), which could result from background features or artifacts being incorrectly interpreted as tumor regions.

Overall, the high classification rates across all categories highlight the model's effectiveness. However, the minor misclassification rates suggest opportunities for improvement, particularly in refining the separation of overlapping features between HGG and LGG. Addressing these issues may involve enhancing the CNN feature extraction stages, fine-tuning the ViT layers, or incorporating additional data preprocessing techniques to minimize noise and improve accuracy.

### 6\. CONCLUSION AND FUTURE WORK

The proposed model demonstrates robust performance by effectively leveraging hierarchical granularity, attention-based feature fusion, and multi-scale information. Features from Brain MRI tumor images are extracted at three granularity levels using DenseNet-201 and then processed through three Vision Transformers, capturing both local and global spatial patterns. The feature fusion technique based on attention incorporates the extracted features that are improved in distinguishing among classes of tumors by focusing on areas that may be relevant for tumor. The fused feature will be classified into HGG, LGG, and No Tumor categories. In that sense, the overall strength of the model developed surpasses the individual performances; whereas DenseNet201 stands with an accuracy of 86% and ViTs stood at 93% respectively. This hybrid approach gives high accuracy and generalization across different tumor types, demonstrating the model's potential as an efficient solution for automated brain tumor diagnosis. Future work will enhance the current model by including interpretability and involve clinician engagement to adopt in clinical settings.

The future work on hybrid architecture for classification of brain tumor will be directed towards the fine-tuning and optimization of the model. Furthermore, combining multiple image modalities, including MRI, PET, and CT, will also be explored for better classification as well as increased performance and stability. To validate the real-world applicability of these models, further research will be conducted to test them in clinical settings, ensuring they perform effectively in diverse patient populations and environments. Furthermore, explainability and interpretability modules will be added to ensure transparency in the decision making. This will enhance trust and facilitate clinical adoption by ensuring that the model’s decisions are not only accurate but also understandable and justifiable.

## Chapter 8

# Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) for Enhanced Decision-Making in Medical Imaging

Kehinde Iyioluwa Adeyinka

[![Orcid Image](image/orcid-logo.png)https://orcid.org/0009-0009-7685-6693](https://orcid.org/0009-0009-7685-6693)

University of Science and Technology, Beijing, China

Taye Iyinoluwa Adeyinka

[![Orcid Image](image/orcid-logo.png)https://orcid.org/0009-0006-4357-6319](https://orcid.org/0009-0006-4357-6319)

University of Science and Technology, Beijing, China

Joseph Wadefai Passing

[![Orcid Image](image/orcid-logo.png)https://orcid.org/0009-0006-7615-6900](https://orcid.org/0009-0006-7615-6900)

University of Science and Technology, Beijing, China

### ABSTRACT

The rapid development in medical imaging technologies has greatly enlarged the capacity to diagnose and treat a wide range of medical diseases. On the other hand, because of the increased complexity and number of medical pictures, it is challenging to provide timely and proper decision-making. Among deep learning methods, CNN has been an auspicious approach in automatically and effectively carrying out medical image analysis, thus enabling faster, more effective, and more reliable diagnostic procedures. This chapter examines the use of CNNs in medical imaging: multi-modal imaging data integration, image segmentation, and the identification of an illness are given special attention. We cover how CNNs can be applied to early diagnosis, augmenting clinical decision-making by capturing delicate patterns that human clinicians may lose. Also, we examine how CNN-based systems support real-time decision-making for emergency diagnosis and robotic surgery.

### 1\. INTRODUCTION

Medical imaging has incredibly changed the healthcare industry with its non-invasive ways of identifying and monitoring various ailments and diseases. Traditional imaging methods, such as CT, MRI, ultrasound, and X-rays, have been crucial in clinical diagnosis for decades. but, the increasing data generation and heightened complexity of medical images has various challenges to healthcare workers. In return, AI systems that can support medical image interpretation have been developed in response to increasing demands for more effective decision-making tools. Convolutional Neural Networks are among the most efficient AI methods, among many other effective methods for automating image analysis.

#### Figure 1. Medical Image Techniques

![](image/979-8-3693-9816-6.ch008.f01.png)

CNNs are a subset of deep learning architectures that are especially well-suited to medical image analysis because of their excellent processing accuracy in visual data. This is because CNNs play a critical role in modern medical imaging, automatically extracting relevant features from images and learning from extensive data to generate predictions with minimal human inpuy ([LeCun, Bengio, & Hinton, 1998](#979-8-3693-9816-6.ch008.bits-pdf.xhtml#_idTextAnchor498)). Yann LeCun and colleagues first developed CNNs to automate image recognition tasks in the early 1990s ([LeCun, Bengio, & Hinton, 2015](#979-8-3693-9816-6.ch008.bits-pdf.xhtml#_idTextAnchor499)). However, CNNs were not widely used in the big data explosion and computer power improvements, especially in the medical imaging industry. Identifying abnormalities in chest X-rays and categorizing brain cancers in MRI scans were among the early uses of CNNs in medical diagnostics ([Shin et al., 2016](#979-8-3693-9816-6.ch008.bits-pdf.xhtml#_idTextAnchor510)). These days, CNNs are used in many different imaging modalities and applications, such as radiology, pathology, dermatology, and ophthalmology.

CNNs' architecture is one of the factors contributing to their success in medical imaging. Convolutional, pooling, and fully connected layers are among the several layers that make up CNNs. These levels enable the network to learn hierarchical feature representations of images automatically. CNNs are very good at diagnosing illnesses from complicated medical images because they can extract features without human assistance ([Aamir et al., 2023](#979-8-3693-9816-6.ch008.bits-pdf.xhtml#_idTextAnchor479)). The increasing flexibility of CNNs has facilitated the application of these models to 3D imaging data, such as the MRI and the CT scans, further increased their applicability within the medical domain. Disease detection is one of the more popular applications of CNNs in medical imaging. Various CNN-based systems have been developed to detect diseases based on medical images, including neurological disorders, cardiovascular conditions, and cancers. For instance, CNNs have been applied in oncology for diagnosing skin cancer from dermatological images ([Aamir et al., 2022](#979-8-3693-9816-6.ch008.bits-pdf.xhtml#_idTextAnchor481)), locating lung cancer from CT scans ([Esteva et al., 2017](#979-8-3693-9816-6.ch008.bits-pdf.xhtml#_idTextAnchor491)), and detecting and classifying tumors from mammography images in breast cancer ([Mridha et al., 2021](#979-8-3693-9816-6.ch008.bits-pdf.xhtml#_idTextAnchor502)). CNNs help improve diagnostic efficiency and reduce work pressure on radiologists by automating detection tasks, therefore making life-threatening conditions recognized more accurately and earlier. Besides, there is enormous potential for CNNs in neurological diagnosis. In neurology, CNN has been used to diagnose the early detection of Alzheimer's disease using MRI images ([Kriegeskorte, 2015](#979-8-3693-9816-6.ch008.bits-pdf.xhtml#_idTextAnchor497)). CNNs have also identified strokes and brain hemorrhages from CT and MRI images, respectively, thus supporting doctors with valuable information in urgent situations where an immediate diagnosis is required ([Rajpurkar et al., 2018](#979-8-3693-9816-6.ch008.bits-pdf.xhtml#_idTextAnchor506)).

In addition to standard radiology, CNNs are being investigated in dermatology, where they assist doctors in identifying skin cancers like melanoma from pictures of skin lesions ([Esteva et al., 2017](#979-8-3693-9816-6.ch008.bits-pdf.xhtml#_idTextAnchor491)). CNNs' capacity to identify patterns in pictures that are hard for the human eye to pick up on can result in quicker and more accurate diagnoses, which could enhance patient outcomes. Image Segmentation and Its Influence on Decision-Making CNNs have significantly impacted even medical image segmentation. Image segmentation, which includes dividing an image into meaningful parts such as organs, tumors, or blood arteries, provides substantial assistance in the diagnosis, treatment planning, and observation of disease courses. Precise segmentation helps clinicians locate, size, and shape a tumor, which is essential in choosing the best course of therapy. CNNs automatically learn and extract features pertinent to the segmentation process, which makes them very useful for medical picture segmentation applications. Conventional picture segmentation methods frequently call for human contributions, which can be laborious and prone to have mistaken. On the other hand, CNN-based segmentation algorithms can effectively process enormous amounts of medical pictures, significantly reducing the time required for diagnosis. Moreover, it has been shown that CNNs outperform the performance of the traditional methods in such applications as detecting liver tumors from CT scans ([Di et al., 2022](#979-8-3693-9816-6.ch008.bits-pdf.xhtml#_idTextAnchor489)), brain tumor segmentation from MRI scans (Guan et al., n.d.), and retinal vascular segmentation in ophthalmology ([Wang et al., 2022](#979-8-3693-9816-6.ch008.bits-pdf.xhtml#_idTextAnchor515)).

The segmentation process done with CNNs makes much of a difference in clinical decision-making. Clinicians can make much better treatment decisions, surgical techniques, and tactics for monitoring, provided the segmentations are more accurate and detailed. For example, proper delineation of tumors for oncological cases helps to plan radiation treatment more precisely, sparing normal tissues and optimizing the dose to the tumor ([Gul & Khan, 2023](#979-8-3693-9816-6.ch008.bits-pdf.xhtml#_idTextAnchor494)). In general, clinical practice, different imaging modalities are combined to provide a more complete picture of a patient's condition. Multi-modality imaging integrates information from various sources- CT, MRI, PET scans, and ultrasound- to give a more enhanced view of the anatomy and pathology. However, combining such imaging modalities has many challenges, especially in co-coordinating the data from several sources and ensuring that the pertinent information is captured. CNNs demonstrate promise in treating such problems by making it possible to fuse multi-modal medical pictures. Multi-modality imaging will enable physicians to exploit the strengths of each imaging modality: PET for metabolic activity, MRI for soft tissue contrast, and CT for comprehensive anatomical information. CNNs can help detect diseases that may not be as apparent if only one imaging modality is used and make more accurate predictions by combining various data. CNNs, for example, have been applied in oncology by combining CT and PET scans to segment and monitor tumor growth ([Liang, Zadeh, & Morency, 2024](#979-8-3693-9816-6.ch008.bits-pdf.xhtml#_idTextAnchor500)). Multi-modal image data integration enhances decision-making by giving physicians a richer understanding of patient conditions. This, in some cases, could lead to improved treatment response monitoring, more accurate tumor staging, and earlier disease detection ([Pei et al., 2023](#979-8-3693-9816-6.ch008.bits-pdf.xhtml#_idTextAnchor505)). Real-time decision-making plays a vital role in medicine, especially in critical care, where immediate diagnosis and treatment are necessary. The CNNs are finding their way into real-time decision-making systems where their accuracy and speed are critical, such as telemedicine platforms, robotic operations, and emergency diagnostics. CNN, can help guide the surgeon during robotic surgery by interpreting real-time visual feeds from surgical cameras and offering information about the surgical site. In order to direct the surgeon's actions appropriately, this can assist in identifying areas of concern, such as tumors or anomalies. Similarly, CNN-based systems can quickly analyze emergency medical pictures for clinicians, who must make quick decisions. Despite the above achievements, several obstacles must be overcome to unleash CNNs completely in medical imaging. One of the significant challenges is the need for extensive datasets with annotations for CNN training. Medical imaging datasets are often limited due to issues with high-quality labelled data, patient consent, and privacy concerns ([Willemink et al., 2020](#979-8-3693-9816-6.ch008.bits-pdf.xhtml#_idTextAnchor516)), according to. Without question, solving this problem and ensuring the safety and ethics in data exchange will require collaboration among medical facilities, researchers, and regulatory agencies. Another challenge is the interpretability of CNN. While CNNs can provide accurate predictions, it is often hard to know from what the model has derived a specific decision ([Alzubaidi et al., 2021](#979-8-3693-9816-6.ch008.bits-pdf.xhtml#_idTextAnchor486)). Accountability and transparency are most important in life-critical healthcare applications; thus, the “black-box” nature of deep learning models raises questions about their application. These challenges notwithstanding, CNNs have a promising future in medical imaging ([Altaf, Shah, et al., 2019](#979-8-3693-9816-6.ch008.bits-pdf.xhtml#_idTextAnchor485))\]. The current limitations cited are expected to be removed by developments in explainable AI, generative models, and transfer learning. Moreover, using CNNs with other innovative technologies, such as robotics, augmented reality (Jayasundar & Kumar, n.d.), and personalized medicine, may transform healthcare delivery in ways never seen before. Indeed, convolutional neural networks have greatly improved decision-making in medical imaging. CNNs are helpful in diverse uses for physicians, such as multi-modal integration, image segmentation, and disease identification and diagnosis ([Xu et al., 2024](#979-8-3693-9816-6.ch008.bits-pdf.xhtml#_idTextAnchor518)). Full integration of CNNs into real-time clinical decision-making and treatment planning is expected to proliferate further. At the same time, AI evolves, leading to better patient outcomes and lower healthcare expenses. In particular, before the CNN-based systems can be safely and effectively used in clinical practice, data accessibility, model interpretability, and regulatory considerations have to be addressed.

#### 1.1 Literature review

Medical imaging has been considered a principal pillar of modern healthcare for several decades, providing doctors of various specialties with diagnostic aids. The demand for image analysis that is more automated, effective, and accurate has increased in the last few decades. Convolutional neural networks (CNNs) are one of the most promising technologies for automated medical image analysis, and their development has been accelerated by this spike in demand ([Aamir et al., 2019](#979-8-3693-9816-6.ch008.bits-pdf.xhtml#_idTextAnchor480)). In image classification, detection, and segmentation tasks all critical for making decisions in medical practice—CNNs, a subset of deep learning algorithms, have shown remarkable performance.

This literature review aims to assess the use of CNNs in medical imaging, underlining advances, challenges, and possible applications of this technology to improve diagnosis and treatment decision-making in illness. The history of CNNs in medical imaging started when LeCun and associates initially created the convolutional architecture for pattern recognition tasks in the 1990s ([LeCun, Bengio, & Hinton, 1998](#979-8-3693-9816-6.ch008.bits-pdf.xhtml#_idTextAnchor498)). Initially, CNNs were applied for non-medical applications such as natural language processing and handwritten digit recognition. Only after significant advances in computational powers and the availability of large datasets could CNNs significantly impact medical imaging ([LeCun, Bengio, & Hinton, 2015](#979-8-3693-9816-6.ch008.bits-pdf.xhtml#_idTextAnchor499)). Currently, CNNs have been used for various tasks spanning disease classification, detection, segmentation, and even prognosis prediction. Since then, their use in the medical profession has proliferated ([Tufail et al., 2021](#979-8-3693-9816-6.ch008.bits-pdf.xhtml#_idTextAnchor513)). Because of their automatic hierarchical extraction from images, CNNs are particularly adept at medical imaging. CNNs can learn spatial hierarchies of features straight from the raw data, unlike standard machine learning models, which have to be hand-engineered by features, as per ([Du et al., 2020](#979-8-3693-9816-6.ch008.bits-pdf.xhtml#_idTextAnchor490)). In medical imaging, where the relevant entities, like cancers, lesions, and organs, may vary in size, shape, and texture between patients, this auto-feature extraction becomes essential. Particular benefits of CNNs show up in radiology, where they have transformed the practice of medicine with their ability to process and interpret images. Applications in radiology focused on the early detection and classification of malignancies present within chest X-rays ([Moses et al., 2021](#979-8-3693-9816-6.ch008.bits-pdf.xhtml#_idTextAnchor501)). The field has since expanded to include a variety of imaging methods, such as MRI, CT, and ultrasound. Indeed, various studies have involved CNNs that outperform human radiologists, particularly in detecting a variety of minor abnormalities that would remain unnoticed otherwise. CNNs' main applications in medical imaging involve the identification and detection of diseases. Deep learning models can leverage the rich information contained in medical images, particularly those generated from radiological methods, for exact disease identification. CNNs are applied to the detection of illnesses in a number of medical conditions, including cancer, neurological disorders, and cardiovascular disorders.

In oncology, CNNs have been applied successfully to detect tumors within MRI, CT, and mammography images. The use of CNNs to identify breast cancer from mammograms is a good example. In the study by ([Oyelade et al., 2022](#979-8-3693-9816-6.ch008.bits-pdf.xhtml#_idTextAnchor504)), CNN-based models could classify mammogram pictures with accuracy that matched that of skilled radiologists. Because of this capacity to identify microcalcifications, masses, and other minute characteristics suggestive of breast cancer, CNNs are very useful in early diagnosis ([Al-Yasriy, et al., 2020](#979-8-3693-9816-6.ch008.bits-pdf.xhtml#_idTextAnchor482)). CNNs have also been used to detect lung cancer from chest CT scans. ([Atmakuru, et al., 2024](#979-8-3693-9816-6.ch008.bits-pdf.xhtml#_idTextAnchor487)) investigated the efficiency of a deep CNN model in detecting lung cancer that could reach the accuracy level of human radiologists. This capacity is beneficial given the complexity and volume of chest CT images that can take much time and experience to examine. Automating the detection process can help reduce the burden on radiologists so that they can have more time for complicated patients or treatments. The CNNs have shown great promise in dermatology for detecting skin cancer from dermatological pictures, particularly melanoma. [Winkler et al. (2023)](#979-8-3693-9816-6.ch008.bits-pdf.xhtml#_idTextAnchor517) showed that CNNs may outperform general practitioners in melanoma detection and classify skin lesions at a dermatologist-level performance. This article points out the potential of CNNs in those specialties where early identification is crucial to successful treatment. CNNs have also been used in neurology to diagnose neurological conditions such as stroke, brain tumors, and Alzheimer's disease ([Gautam & Sharma, 2020](#979-8-3693-9816-6.ch008.bits-pdf.xhtml#_idTextAnchor493)). For instance, CNNs, when applied to MRI images, have shown great promise in detecting early signs of Alzheimer's disease ([Yao, et al., 2023](#979-8-3693-9816-6.ch008.bits-pdf.xhtml#_idTextAnchor519)). One of CNNs' main capabilities is their ability to detect very slight changes in brain morphology, such as atrophy of the hippocampus. Such a possibility will significantly enhance early diagnosis and treatment planning. Another important domain in which CNNs' performance has significantly enhanced medical imaging is image segmentation. Segmentation refers to dividing an image into helpful regions, where one might identify specific organs, tumors, or lesions within medical images. Accurate segmentation is important for clinical decision-making in oncology, neurology, and cardiology, where precise demarcation of abnormal tissues plays a key role in diagnosis, treatment planning, and follow-up.

Conventional image segmentation techniques, that depends on physicians' manual demarcation, can be laborious and has no error. Conversely, CNN-based segmentation algorithms automate this procedure, yielding precise and repeatable outcomes that can save significant time in clinical settings ([Xu et al., 2024](#979-8-3693-9816-6.ch008.bits-pdf.xhtml#_idTextAnchor518)). For example, CNNs have been successfully applied to the segmentation of liver lesions in CT images, brain tumors in MRI scans ([Almotairi, et al., 2020](#979-8-3693-9816-6.ch008.bits-pdf.xhtml#_idTextAnchor483)), and retinal vessels in ophthalmology ([Guthoff, et al., 1991](#979-8-3693-9816-6.ch008.bits-pdf.xhtml#_idTextAnchor496)). In all these cases, CNNs outperformed traditional segmentation methods, providing more accurate and reproducible results. CNN-based segmentation bears great impact on clinical decisions. Accurate tumor segmentation in oncology is important to determine tumors’ location, size, and shape, all of which are critical factors for treatment planning. For example, during radiotherapy, correct tumor delineation ensures that radiation hits the right place while reducing maximum injury to healthy tissues ([Burnet, et al., 2004](#979-8-3693-9816-6.ch008.bits-pdf.xhtml#_idTextAnchor488)). In neurology, accurate brain tumor segmentation can be used to guide surgical planning and to improve the monitoring of disease progression. Retinal vascular segmentation is essential in ophthalmology for diagnosing glaucoma and diabetic retinopathy, which can cause blindness if neglected. Another exciting recent development in the field of medical imaging is the integration of multimodal imaging techniques. These techniques can combine data from different multiples imaging modalities to produce a more rounded view of a patient's state. Multimodal imaging provides complementary information, like anatomical, functional, and metabolic data, that forms the basis for accurate diagnosis and treatment planning. Because CNNs can learn characteristics from different sources, they are particularly well-suited to multimodal medical imaging. For example, CNNs have been applied to combine the functional information of PET with the complete anatomical information of CT scans for cancer diagnosis ([Sibille, et al., 2020](#979-8-3693-9816-6.ch008.bits-pdf.xhtml#_idTextAnchor511)). This integration will lead to more personalized treatment regimens due to its improved diagnosis and staging of tumors. CNNs have been applied to neurology for integrating images from PET and MRI to diagnose Alzheimer's disease. Combining structural MRI, which provides accurate anatomical information, with functional PET, which assesses metabolic activity, allows for the detection of early degenerative changes in the brain that may not be visible on any one scan ([Teune, et al., 2010](#979-8-3693-9816-6.ch008.bits-pdf.xhtml#_idTextAnchor512)). Multi-modal imaging data can be integrated by CNNs, by offering a comprehensive view of the patient's state and this enhances clinical decision-making.

Real-time decision-making is integral to several therapeutic situations, mainly telemedicine, emergency care, and surgery. CNNs are increasingly being integrated into real-time decision-making systems like robotic surgery, emergency diagnostics, and telemedicine applications. In robotic surgery, CNNs can be applied to live video feeds from surgical cameras and supply doctors with real-time suggestions about the same.
