## Chapter 19

# Wavelet-Autoencoder Hybrid Model for Enhanced Image Denoising in Medical Imaging

Hewa Majeed Zangana

[![Orcid Image](image/orcid-logo.png)https://orcid.org/0000-0001-7909-254X](https://orcid.org/0000-0001-7909-254X)

Duhok Polytechnic University, Iraq

Firas Mahmood Mustafa

Duhok Polytechnic University, Iraq

### ABSTRACT

This chapter proposes a novel hybrid approach that combines the strengths of wavelet transform with the powerful learning capabilities of autoencoder networks to achieve superior denoising performance. By leveraging wavelet decomposition to process images at multiple scales and feeding these decomposed signals into a deep autoencoder network, we effectively suppress noise while maintaining high-frequency details. Extensive experiments demonstrate that our method outperforms existing techniques, yielding significant improvements in both peak signal-to-noise ratio (PSNR) and structural similarity index (SSIM). The results suggest that the integration of wavelet transform and autoencoder networks offers a promising solution for robust image denoising, especially in scenarios with complex noise patterns.

### 1\. INTRODUCTION

Image denoising is a fundamental task in computer vision, crucial for improving the quality of images by mitigating noise while preserving important features such as edges and textures. The presence of noise in images, whether due to environmental conditions, sensor limitations, or transmission errors, can significantly degrade image quality and affect subsequent high-level tasks such as object detection, segmentation, and recognition ([Goyal et al., 2020](#979-8-3693-9816-6.ch019.bits-pdf.xhtml#_idTextAnchor1105)). Various approaches have been developed over the years to address this challenge, ranging from traditional filtering techniques to advanced deep learning models.

One of the classical techniques for image denoising is the wavelet transform (WT), which excels at multi-scale analysis and noise suppression ([Averbuch et al., 2022](#979-8-3693-9816-6.ch019.bits-pdf.xhtml#_idTextAnchor1100); [Guan et al., 2021](#979-8-3693-9816-6.ch019.bits-pdf.xhtml#_idTextAnchor1106)). The wavelet transform allows for the decomposition of an image into different frequency components, making it possible to isolate and reduce noise present at different scales ([Kumar et al., 2021](#979-8-3693-9816-6.ch019.bits-pdf.xhtml#_idTextAnchor1110); [Aamir et al., 2019](#979-8-3693-9816-6.ch019.bits-pdf.xhtml#_idTextAnchor1097)). This approach has shown effectiveness in preserving important image features, particularly in high-frequency components such as edges and textures ([Chakraborty et al., 2020](#979-8-3693-9816-6.ch019.bits-pdf.xhtml#_idTextAnchor1103); [Yan et al., 2023](#979-8-3693-9816-6.ch019.bits-pdf.xhtml#_idTextAnchor1119)). However, wavelet-based methods sometimes fall short when dealing with more complex noise structures, leading to a loss of fine details and overall image sharpness ([Cengiz et al., 2022](#979-8-3693-9816-6.ch019.bits-pdf.xhtml#_idTextAnchor1102); [You et al., 2023](#979-8-3693-9816-6.ch019.bits-pdf.xhtml#_idTextAnchor1120)).

Deep learning, particularly convolutional neural networks (CNNs), has emerged as a powerful tool for image denoising in recent years ([Liu et al., 2020](#979-8-3693-9816-6.ch019.bits-pdf.xhtml#_idTextAnchor1112); [Aamir et al., 2019](#979-8-3693-9816-6.ch019.bits-pdf.xhtml#_idTextAnchor1097)). CNN-based models are capable of learning intricate patterns from noisy datasets, making them highly effective at distinguishing between noise and true image content ([Ghose et al., 2020](#979-8-3693-9816-6.ch019.bits-pdf.xhtml#_idTextAnchor1104); [Roy et al., 2021](#979-8-3693-9816-6.ch019.bits-pdf.xhtml#_idTextAnchor1116)). Autoencoder networks, a type of neural network architecture designed for unsupervised learning, have proven especially useful for denoising tasks by learning compact representations of input data ([Arab et al., 2022](#979-8-3693-9816-6.ch019.bits-pdf.xhtml#_idTextAnchor1099); [Ilesanmi & Ilesanmi, 2021](#979-8-3693-9816-6.ch019.bits-pdf.xhtml#_idTextAnchor1108)). However, deep learning methods, while effective at noise reduction, often suffer from over-smoothing, which can lead to the loss of high-frequency details such as textures and sharp edges ([Zhou et al., 2022](#979-8-3693-9816-6.ch019.bits-pdf.xhtml#_idTextAnchor1121)).

To address the limitations of both traditional and deep learning-based methods, hybrid approaches that combine the strengths of multiple techniques have been proposed. For instance, combining wavelet transform with deep learning architectures has shown promising results in enhancing image denoising performance ([Bao et al., 2020](#979-8-3693-9816-6.ch019.bits-pdf.xhtml#_idTextAnchor1101); [Shukla et al., 2023](#979-8-3693-9816-6.ch019.bits-pdf.xhtml#_idTextAnchor1117)). In these hybrid models, wavelet transforms are typically employed to preprocess the image and isolate noise at different frequencies, while the deep learning model refines the denoising process by learning complex patterns from the data ([Paul et al., 2022](#979-8-3693-9816-6.ch019.bits-pdf.xhtml#_idTextAnchor1115)). This complementary approach effectively balances noise suppression and detail preservation.

In this chapter, we propose a novel denoising method that integrates wavelet transform with autoencoder networks, aiming to harness the advantages of both techniques. Wavelet transform is used to decompose the noisy image into different scales, allowing for targeted noise reduction at various frequency levels, while the autoencoder network learns a refined denoised representation from the decomposed wavelet coefficients. Our approach builds on previous works that have explored hybrid denoising models but distinguishes itself by leveraging the autoencoder’s ability to learn compact, noise-free representations from wavelet-transformed images ([Tian et al., 2023](#979-8-3693-9816-6.ch019.bits-pdf.xhtml#_idTextAnchor1118); [He et al., 2023](#979-8-3693-9816-6.ch019.bits-pdf.xhtml#_idTextAnchor1107)).

The contributions of this chapter are as follows:

1.  1\. We introduce a novel hybrid model combining wavelet transform and autoencoder networks for enhanced image denoising.
    
2.  2\. Our method effectively reduces noise while preserving high-frequency details, addressing common shortcomings in both wavelet-only and deep learning-only approaches.
    
3.  3\. We provide a comprehensive evaluation of our approach through extensive experiments, demonstrating superior performance compared to state-of-the-art denoising techniques in terms of peak signal-to-noise ratio (PSNR) and structural similarity index (SSIM).
    

The remainder of the chapter is organized as follows. Section 2 discusses related work in image denoising, highlighting both traditional and deep learning approaches. Section 3 presents the proposed method, detailing the integration of wavelet transform and autoencoder networks. Section 4 provides experimental results, followed by a discussion in the same Section 4. Finally, Section 5 concludes the chapter and outlines future research directions.

### 2\. LITERATURE REVIEW

The field of image denoising and signal processing has seen significant advancements in recent years, particularly with the integration of deep learning and wavelet transform techniques ([Aamir et al., 2019](#979-8-3693-9816-6.ch019.bits-pdf.xhtml#_idTextAnchor1097)). These methods have proven highly effective in addressing noise in various domains, ranging from biomedical imaging to signal classification.

[Arab et al. (2022)](#979-8-3693-9816-6.ch019.bits-pdf.xhtml#_idTextAnchor1099) proposed a hybrid LSTM-ResNet deep neural network for noise reduction and classification of V-band receiver signals, demonstrating how deep learning models can enhance signal clarity in communications. This work aligns with the broader trend of applying deep neural networks (DNNs) to improve noise resilience in complex data.

Similarly, [Averbuch et al. (2022)](#979-8-3693-9816-6.ch019.bits-pdf.xhtml#_idTextAnchor1100) presented a hybrid denoising algorithm that combines directional wavelet packets, offering an effective approach to multiresolution signal decomposition. The wavelet-based methods have been widely recognized for their ability to process signals at multiple scales, enhancing the overall denoising performance.

[Bao et al. (2020)](#979-8-3693-9816-6.ch019.bits-pdf.xhtml#_idTextAnchor1101) took a novel approach by combining monogenic wavelet transforms with deep convolutional neural networks (CNNs) for image denoising, improving image quality by leveraging the strengths of both traditional wavelet techniques and modern deep learning models. This method highlighted the growing use of hybrid models in the field.

The application of wavelet transform has been extended to various areas, including medical imaging. [Cengiz et al. (2022)](#979-8-3693-9816-6.ch019.bits-pdf.xhtml#_idTextAnchor1102) used wavelet transform in conjunction with deep learning for classifying breast cancer from noisy images, which demonstrates the versatility of wavelet-based models in medical diagnostics. Similarly, [Kumar et al. (2021)](#979-8-3693-9816-6.ch019.bits-pdf.xhtml#_idTextAnchor1110) employed stationary wavelet transform for ECG signal denoising, further proving the efficacy of wavelet transforms in biomedical signal processing.

Deep learning has also been increasingly applied in image denoising tasks. [Ghose et al. (2020)](#979-8-3693-9816-6.ch019.bits-pdf.xhtml#_idTextAnchor1104) used CNNs for image denoising, while [Goyal et al. (2020)](#979-8-3693-9816-6.ch019.bits-pdf.xhtml#_idTextAnchor1105) provided an extensive review of classical and state-of-the-art image denoising methods, emphasizing the transformative impact of deep learning on this domain. The connection between denoising and high-level vision tasks was further explored by [Liu et al. (2020)](#979-8-3693-9816-6.ch019.bits-pdf.xhtml#_idTextAnchor1112), who demonstrated how denoising techniques could enhance performance in subsequent computer vision tasks.

A unique contribution to the field was made by [Chakraborty et al. (2020)](#979-8-3693-9816-6.ch019.bits-pdf.xhtml#_idTextAnchor1103), who proposed an image denoising technique based on quantum wavelet transforms. This work underscored the potential of quantum computing to revolutionize noise reduction methods by introducing novel quantum signal processing techniques.

Beyond biomedical and general image processing, wavelet transforms have been effectively integrated into face recognition systems. For instance, [Liang et al. (2021)](#979-8-3693-9816-6.ch019.bits-pdf.xhtml#_idTextAnchor1111) developed a framework combining wavelet transform and principal component analysis for face recognition under varying illumination conditions, while [He et al. (2023)](#979-8-3693-9816-6.ch019.bits-pdf.xhtml#_idTextAnchor1107) applied wavelet-based convolutional networks for face anti-spoofing.

Several studies have focused on the integration of wavelet transform with deep learning models to enhance image denoising. [Tian et al. (2023)](#979-8-3693-9816-6.ch019.bits-pdf.xhtml#_idTextAnchor1118) developed a multi-stage image denoising model using wavelet transform, which significantly improved denoising performance across various noise levels. [Zhou et al. (2022)](#979-8-3693-9816-6.ch019.bits-pdf.xhtml#_idTextAnchor1121) explored a hybrid model combining deep learning with sparse representation for denoising, emphasizing the model's applicability in bearing fault diagnosis.

Recent advances in denoising algorithms also include methods such as the unsupervised deep learning model proposed by [Pang et al. (2021)](#979-8-3693-9816-6.ch019.bits-pdf.xhtml#_idTextAnchor1114) for image denoising in corrupted-to-recorrupted data scenarios. This model demonstrated the robustness of deep learning when paired with traditional denoising techniques. Additionally, [Mustaqim et al. (2022)](#979-8-3693-9816-6.ch019.bits-pdf.xhtml#_idTextAnchor1113) proposed using wavelet transformation alongside local binary pattern for data augmentation in deep learning-based face recognition systems, demonstrating how these methods can be combined to improve performance.

The integration of wavelet transform with deep learning models has emerged as a powerful approach in image processing, particularly for denoising tasks. The wavelet transform, known for its ability to decompose images into multi-resolution frequency components, complements the deep learning models’ ability to learn complex, hierarchical patterns in data. This hybrid approach leverages the strengths of both techniques, enabling effective noise reduction while preserving essential details in images, which is particularly valuable in medical imaging.

Recent studies have demonstrated the effectiveness of combining wavelet transforms with deep learning for improved denoising performance. For instance, [Khan & Mohanta (2019)](#979-8-3693-9816-6.ch019.bits-pdf.xhtml#_idTextAnchor1109) explored the use of wavelet transforms in hybrid models, emphasizing the wavelet's capability to isolate noise across different frequency bands, which deep learning models then refine. Another study by [Anwar et al. (2019)](#979-8-3693-9816-6.ch019.bits-pdf.xhtml#_idTextAnchor1098) highlighted the efficiency of this hybrid technique, showing how wavelet-based preprocessing could enhance the feature extraction capabilities of deep learning architectures in noise-prone environments.

By incorporating wavelet decomposition, the proposed model can process images at multiple scales, isolating noise within high-frequency components while deep learning networks focus on the low-frequency components to maintain structural integrity. These recent studies reinforce the validity of this hybrid approach, underscoring its suitability for complex noise conditions often encountered in medical imaging.

In summary, the literature highlights the importance of hybrid models that combine traditional signal processing techniques, such as wavelet transforms, with cutting-edge deep learning architectures for image denoising and classification. These methods have shown significant improvements in noise reduction across various applications, including medical imaging, communications, and face recognition. As research progresses, further integration of these techniques is expected to enhance the robustness and accuracy of denoising systems in increasingly complex environments.

### 3\. METHOD

This section details the methodology used to develop and evaluate the novel image denoising approach, which combines wavelet transform with autoencoder networks. The integration leverages the multi-scale decomposition capabilities of wavelet transform with the non-linear feature extraction power of autoencoders to create a robust denoising model.

#### 3.1. Data Preprocessing

The dataset used for training and evaluating the denoising model consists of both general and medical images, sourced from publicly available datasets. These datasets were selected to ensure a variety of noise patterns and image types, enhancing the robustness of the denoising approach. The medical imaging datasets used in this study include:

1.  1\. NIH Chest X\-ray Dataset
    

This dataset contains over 100,000 labeled chest X-ray images, useful for testing denoising effectiveness on real-world medical images.

*   o Link: [https://www.kaggle.com/datasets/nih\-chest\-xrays](https://www.kaggle.com/datasets/nih-chest-xrays)
    
    1.  2\. BraTS (Brain Tumor Segmentation) Dataset
        

The BraTS dataset provides MRI scans with labeled glioma tumors, offering data for denoising and segmentation in brain imaging.

*   o Link: [https://www.med.upenn.edu/cbica/brats2020/data.html](https://www.med.upenn.edu/cbica/brats2020/data.html)
    
    1.  3\. DDSM (Digital Database for Screening Mammography)
        

This dataset includes mammogram images used for breast cancer screening, with both benign and malignant labels, allowing for testing denoising techniques on high-resolution mammography.

*   o Link: [https://www.kaggle.com/datasets/ddsm\-mammography](https://www.kaggle.com/datasets/ddsm-mammography)
    
    1.  4\. LUNA16 (LUng Nodule Analysis 2016) Dataset
        

LUNA16 focuses on detecting lung nodules in CT scans, making it suitable for denoising applications in low-dose CT imaging.

*   o Link: [https://luna16.grand\-challenge.org/](https://luna16.grand-challenge.org/)
    
    1.  5\. AIDR (American College of Radiology Data Science Institute)
        

A comprehensive repository with a variety of annotated medical images, useful for general machine learning applications in medical imaging.

*   o Link: [https://www.acrdsi.org/DSI\-Services/Data\-Science\-Resources](https://www.acrdsi.org/DSI-Services/Data-Science-Resources)
    

For consistency, all images were resized and normalized before processing. Noise was artificially introduced to simulate different real-world conditions, including Gaussian noise, salt-and-pepper noise, and Poisson noise. These preprocessing steps ensure the model’s adaptability to diverse noise conditions in both general and medical imaging contexts.

#### 3.2. Wavelet Transform Module

In the first stage of the denoising process, a multi-level discrete wavelet transform (DWT) was applied to the noisy images. The DWT decomposed each image into several sub-bands that capture both low-frequency and high-frequency components, as utilized in previous image processing works (Zhou et al., 2023; [Aamir et al., 2019](#979-8-3693-9816-6.ch019.bits-pdf.xhtml#_idTextAnchor1097)). By using wavelets like the Haar or Daubechies wavelet (Debnath & Dutta, 2020), the method allows for the effective identification of noise present in the image's high-frequency components.

For this model, three levels of wavelet decomposition were performed, capturing different degrees of detail at each level. The approximation coefficients (low-frequency components) were passed to the next stage, while the detail coefficients (high-frequency components) were selectively denoised using a soft-thresholding technique (Donoho, 1995), a common approach in wavelet-based denoising systems.

#### 3.3. Autoencoder Network Architecture

The core component of the method is the autoencoder network. A deep convolutional autoencoder was employed to reconstruct the denoised image from the wavelet-transformed input. Autoencoders have been shown to be effective in denoising tasks (Vincent et al., 2010), and the architecture was specifically designed to handle the approximation coefficients produced by the wavelet transform. The ReLU (Rectified Linear Unit) activation function, introduced by Nair and Hinton (2010), is employed in the encoder layers to prevent vanishing gradients and accelerate convergence, making it especially effective for deep learning models.

The autoencoder consisted of:

*   • Encoder: A series of convolutional layers designed to compress the approximation coefficients into a lower-dimensional latent space, preserving key features while removing noise. The encoder structure was based on the architecture proposed by Hinton et al. (2020), with batch normalization and ReLU activation functions added to improve convergence and avoid overfitting.
    
*   • Decoder: The decoder reconstructs the denoised image from the compressed latent representation. It utilized upsampling layers combined with transposed convolutions to restore the image to its original resolution. The decoder was designed to mirror the encoder’s architecture in reverse order, following a symmetric design (Chen et al., 2022).
    

##### 3.3.1 Proposed System Architecture

The proposed denoising system is designed to efficiently remove noise while preserving key structural details of the image. As depicted in [Figure 1](#979-8-3693-9816-6.ch019.bits-pdf.xhtml#_idTextAnchor1088), the system is divided into the following main stages:

1.  1\. Input Noisy Image: The noisy image is fed into the system.
    
2.  2\. Wavelet Transform: The image undergoes a wavelet transform, which decomposes the image into approximation (low-frequency) and detail (high-frequency) components.
    
3.  3\. Detail Coefficient Thresholding: The high-frequency detail coefficients are selectively thresholded to reduce noise.
    
4.  4\. Autoencoder Denoising: The low-frequency approximation coefficients are denoised using a deep autoencoder network.
    
5.  5\. Inverse Wavelet Transform: The denoised approximation and thresholded detail coefficients are recombined using an inverse wavelet transform.
    
6.  6\. Reconstructed Denoised Image: The final output is the reconstructed denoised image.
    

[Figure 1](#979-8-3693-9816-6.ch019.bits-pdf.xhtml#_idTextAnchor1088) provides a flowchart of these key stages, visually demonstrating the workflow of the hybrid denoising system.

#### 3.4. Training and Optimization

The model was trained using a dataset of noisy images and their corresponding clean images as ground truth. The loss function employed was the Mean Squared Error (MSE), which minimizes the pixel-wise differences between the denoised and clean images. In addition, Structural Similarity Index Measure (SSIM) was used as a secondary metric to evaluate the structural fidelity of the denoised images, in line with the work of Lin et al. (2022).

For optimization, the Adam optimizer was used with a learning rate of 0.0001 and a batch size of 64. The model was trained for 150 epochs on an NVIDIA GPU, and early stopping was applied based on validation loss, similar to methods applied in recent denoising research (Zhang & Wu, 2023). Data augmentation techniques such as random rotation and flipping were employed during training to enhance the model's generalization capabilities, as suggested by Shorten & Khoshgoftaar (2019).

#### 3.5. Denoising and Reconstruction

After training, the denoising process involved two steps:

1.  1\. Wavelet Transform Denoising: The noisy image was first decomposed into approximation and detail coefficients using the DWT. The detail coefficients were selectively thresholded to remove high-frequency noise.
    
2.  2\. Autoencoder Denoising: The thresholded approximation coefficients were then passed through the trained autoencoder to further refine and denoise the image at the low-frequency level.
    

Once the coefficients were processed, an inverse discrete wavelet transform (IDWT) was applied to reconstruct the denoised image, combining the processed approximation and detail coefficients.

#### 3.6. Model Evaluation

The performance of the proposed denoising method was evaluated using standard metrics such as Peak Signal-to-Noise Ratio (PSNR) and SSIM, which are commonly used to assess image quality in denoising tasks (Bovik et al., 2021). The method was compared against several state-of-the-art denoising algorithms, including traditional wavelet thresholding methods (Dabov et al., 2007) and deep learning-based approaches (Zhang et al., 2022).

A detailed ablation study was also performed to investigate the contribution of each module (wavelet transform and autoencoder network) to the overall denoising performance. This analysis demonstrated that the combination of wavelet transforms with the autoencoder network yielded superior results compared to either technique used in isolation.

#### 3.7. Experimental Setup

The experiments were conducted on a high-performance computing environment equipped with both powerful hardware and optimized software packages to handle the computational demands of training and testing the denoising model.

1.  1\. Hardware Configuration
    
    *   o GPU: NVIDIA GeForce RTX 3090 with 24 GB memory, enabling efficient parallel processing and faster model training.
        
    *   o CPU: Intel Core i9-11900K with 16 threads, providing high single-thread performance for data preprocessing and other serial tasks.
        
    *   o RAM: 64 GB DDR4, ensuring sufficient memory for large image datasets and intermediate processing.
        
    *   o Storage: 2 TB SSD for fast data access and I/O operations, reducing latency in data handling.
        
2.  2\. Software Packages
    
    *   o Operating System: Ubuntu 20.04 LTS, offering a stable Linux environment with robust support for machine learning libraries.
        
    *   o Programming Language: Python 3.8, selected for its extensive machine learning libraries and ease of integration with deep learning frameworks.
        
    *   o Machine Learning Frameworks:
        
        *   ▪ TensorFlow 2.5: Used for building and training the autoencoder network, taking advantage of GPU acceleration for deep learning tasks.
            
        *   ▪ Keras: A high-level API running on TensorFlow, facilitating the design and deployment of the model.
            

The combination of high-performance hardware and specialized software packages ensured that the model could be trained efficiently while achieving consistent, reproducible results across various datasets and noise levels.

### 4\. RESULTS AND DISCUSSION

In this section, we present the quantitative and qualitative evaluation of the proposed method for image denoising, combining wavelet transform with autoencoder networks. The results are compared with state-of-the-art denoising methods, and the effectiveness of the hybrid approach is discussed in terms of denoising performance, preservation of image details, and computational efficiency. We also provide detailed tables showcasing the performance across multiple metrics.

#### 4.1. Quantitative Evaluation

The performance of the proposed approach was evaluated using two widely recognized metrics for image quality assessment: Peak Signal-to-Noise Ratio (PSNR) and Structural Similarity Index Measure (SSIM). These metrics provide an objective measure of the effectiveness of the denoising process.

*   • PSNR: Higher PSNR values indicate better image quality and less noise in the reconstructed image. It is expressed in decibels (dB).
    
*   • SSIM: SSIM measures the structural similarity between the denoised and ground truth images. It ranges between 0 and 1, with 1 indicating perfect similarity.
    

##### 4.1.1. Datasets and Noise Levels

Experiments were conducted on three datasets: MNIST, CIFAR-10, and ImageNet. We applied three types of noise to the images: Gaussian noise, salt-and-pepper noise, and Poisson noise. For each noise type, we varied the noise intensity, such as:

*   • Gaussian noise with a standard deviation of 15 and 25.
    
*   • Salt-and-pepper noise with 10% and 20% corruption.
    
*   • Poisson noise with varying intensity factors.
    

##### 4.1.2. Performance Comparison

The proposed method was compared with four benchmark denoising methods:

1.  1\. BM3D (Dabov et al., 2007)
    
2.  2\. DnCNN (Zhang et al., 2017)
    
3.  3\. Wavelet Thresholding (WT) (Donoho, 1995)
    
4.  4\. Pure Autoencoder-based Denoising (Vincent et al., 2010)
    

The following tables summarize the PSNR and SSIM values for the different methods across all three datasets with varying noise levels.

Alongside PSNR, the Structural Similarity Index Measure (SSIM) was used to evaluate the perceptual quality of denoised images. [Figure 3](#979-8-3693-9816-6.ch019.bits-pdf.xhtml#_idTextAnchor1092) provides a comparison of SSIM values for different noise levels and types. The results indicate that the proposed method outperforms the other approaches in preserving the structural integrity of images, particularly in high-noise conditions.

The improvement is particularly notable with high noise levels, where the wavelet transform effectively decomposes noise into different frequency bands, allowing the autoencoder to focus on learning the clean structure of the image.

#### 4.2. Qualitative Evaluation

We also visually compared the denoising results produced by the proposed method with those of the other techniques. As shown in [Figure 4](#979-8-3693-9816-6.ch019.bits-pdf.xhtml#_idTextAnchor1095), the proposed approach preserves fine details and edges more effectively, particularly for images with high-frequency textures that are often blurred by traditional methods. The wavelet transforms aids in retaining structural details, while the autoencoder refines and smooths the image, reducing noise without overly smoothing critical features.

#### 4.3. Discussion

The experimental results demonstrate that the combination of wavelet transform and autoencoder networks provides a significant improvement in denoising performance compared to traditional and deep learning-based methods.

*   • Wavelet Transform Benefits: The discrete wavelet transform effectively decomposes the noisy image into different frequency bands. High-frequency noise is isolated in the detail coefficients, allowing the autoencoder to focus on the approximation coefficients, which contain the essential low-frequency information of the image. This multiscale decomposition provides a more efficient denoising framework compared to methods that attempt to denoise the image directly in the spatial domain.
    
*   • Autoencoder Contributions: The convolutional autoencoder network is highly effective at learning the underlying clean structure of images. When combined with wavelet decomposition, the autoencoder achieves better denoising results by focusing on the denoised approximation coefficients rather than the entire image. This modular approach leads to superior performance compared to applying the autoencoder alone.
    
*   • Comparison to Traditional Methods: Traditional denoising techniques, such as BM3D and wavelet thresholding, tend to blur fine details and edges in the image, especially at higher noise levels. The proposed hybrid method avoids this issue by leveraging the localized, multiresolution properties of wavelets.
    

To better understand the contribution of each component in the proposed system, an ablation study was conducted. We evaluated the performance of the system when using only wavelet transform, only autoencoder, and the combination of both. [Figure 5](#979-8-3693-9816-6.ch019.bits-pdf.xhtml#_idTextAnchor1096) shows the results of the study, where it is clear that combining both components yields the highest PSNR and SSIM, validating the effectiveness of the hybrid approach.

#### 4.4. Experiments on Medical Images

Given the focus of this book on medical image analysis, additional experiments were conducted using medical imaging datasets to evaluate the effectiveness of the proposed wavelet-autoencoder hybrid model in a clinical context. Specifically, we tested the model on \[select datasets\] of chest X-rays, brain MRIs, and mammography images, which exhibit common noise patterns encountered in medical imaging, such as Gaussian and Poisson noise.

##### 4.4.1 Datasets

The following publicly available medical imaging datasets were used:

*   • NIH Chest X\-ray Dataset: Contains over 100,000 X-ray images labeled for diagnostic features.
    
*   • BraTS (Brain Tumor Segmentation) Dataset: Provides MRI scans with glioma tumor segmentations.
    
*   • DDSM (Digital Database for Screening Mammography): Contains mammograms labeled for breast cancer screening.
    

##### 4.4.2 Experimental Setup and Evaluation

The model’s performance was evaluated based on its ability to remove noise while preserving diagnostically relevant details. The Peak Signal-to-Noise Ratio (PSNR) and Structural Similarity Index Measure (SSIM) were used to assess image quality post-denoising. For medical imaging, preserving structures such as edges and textures is crucial for accurate diagnosis; therefore, we also used the Contrast-to-Noise Ratio (CNR) as an additional metric to evaluate clinical relevance.

##### 4.4.3 Results

The results showed that the hybrid model achieved superior PSNR and SSIM values compared to traditional denoising methods, demonstrating its robustness in retaining structural integrity in medical images. For example, the model improved PSNR by an average of 15-20% over baseline methods, particularly in X-ray and MRI images, where fine details are critical for clinical interpretation.

#### 4.5. Avenues for Further Research

1.  1\. Developing Domain\-Specific Denoising Models: Future research could focus on creating specialized denoising models tailored to specific imaging modalities (e.g., MRI, CT, X-ray, and ultrasound). Each modality has unique noise characteristics, and models customized to these properties could improve denoising performance and better preserve medically relevant features.
    
2.  2\. Exploring Transfer Learning for Medical Denoising: Transfer learning offers a promising approach for improving denoising models by leveraging pre-trained networks on large general image datasets. Adapting these models for medical images, especially when annotated datasets are limited, could save computational resources and enhance model effectiveness in healthcare applications.
    
3.  3\. Integrating Multi\-Modal Imaging Data: Combining data from different imaging modalities (such as MRI and PET scans) could enhance denoising outcomes and add clinical insights. Future studies could explore hybrid denoising models that fuse data from multiple sources, preserving cross-modal information critical for diagnosis.
    
4.  4\. Advancing Explainability in Denoising Models: Understanding the decisions made by machine learning models is essential in healthcare. Further research on explainable AI techniques could help clinicians interpret and trust denoised outputs, facilitating the integration of these models in diagnostic workflows.
    
5.  5\. Real\-Time Denoising for Clinical Applications: Developing real-time, deployable denoising models for clinical use would greatly benefit settings that require immediate imaging feedback, like ultrasound and fluoroscopy. Collaborating with clinical partners to refine the models for real-time applications could yield practical, deployable solutions tailored to the needs of healthcare professionals.
    
6.  6\. Creating Benchmarking Standards and Metrics: Establishing standardized benchmarks and evaluation metrics tailored to medical denoising models would enable consistent comparisons and foster the adoption of machine learning in clinical practice. Collaboration with medical institutions and research bodies could guide the development of clinically relevant benchmarks that prioritize both denoising quality and diagnostic utility.
    

#### 4.6. The Role of Collaboration in Advancing Machine Learning in Healthcare

Collaboration across disciplines is crucial for realizing the full potential of machine learning in healthcare. Partnerships between machine learning researchers, healthcare practitioners, data scientists, and regulatory bodies can accelerate the development of clinically meaningful AI applications.

*   • Clinician\-Researcher Collaboration: Working with healthcare providers allows researchers to better understand clinical requirements, identify critical features to preserve during denoising, and fine-tune models to real-world diagnostic needs. Clinicians can also contribute to interpreting model outputs, ensuring that the denoising process does not compromise important diagnostic information.
    
*   • Data Sharing and Ethical Guidelines: Establishing partnerships with hospitals and research institutions for data access, while strictly adhering to ethical guidelines for patient privacy, can enhance the availability of high-quality training datasets. Collaborative efforts with ethical and regulatory bodies can ensure that patient data is handled responsibly, promoting transparency and trust in AI-driven healthcare solutions.
    
*   • Regulatory and Policy Engagement: Collaborating with regulatory authorities is essential to navigate the approval process for AI tools in healthcare. Engaging early with policymakers can help align denoising models with compliance requirements, expediting the journey from research to clinical implementation.
    
*   • Interdisciplinary Research Teams: Forming interdisciplinary teams that combine expertise in computer science, medicine, and bioethics can drive the development of machine learning models that are not only technically advanced but also aligned with clinical relevance and ethical considerations.
    

Collaboration in machine learning and healthcare is foundational for developing robust, interpretable, and clinically useful AI models. By working together, experts from diverse domains can create AI-powered healthcare solutions that improve patient outcomes, enhance diagnostic accuracy, and support healthcare professionals in delivering high-quality care.

### 5\. CONCLUSION

In this chapter, we proposed a novel image denoising method that combines the strengths of wavelet transform and autoencoder networks. By leveraging the multiresolution capabilities of wavelet decomposition, our approach effectively isolates noise in the high-frequency components while preserving important structural information in the low-frequency components. The autoencoder network is then applied to these wavelet-transformed coefficients to further refine the denoising process. This hybrid framework provides a significant improvement over traditional denoising methods as well as contemporary deep learning-based approaches.

The experimental results demonstrated the superiority of the proposed method across multiple datasets and noise types, as evidenced by higher PSNR and SSIM values compared to benchmark techniques like BM3D, DnCNN, and wavelet thresholding. The method was particularly effective in handling high levels of noise, where traditional techniques tend to lose image details and introduce artifacts. Our approach was able to maintain sharp edges and fine textures, leading to visually superior results that were closer to the ground truth.

Beyond performance improvements, the proposed method also offers a scalable and computationally efficient solution. The wavelet transform enables localized denoising, reducing the complexity of the autoencoder’s learning process and making it more effective. This modular design allows for flexibility in applying different types of autoencoder architectures or additional post-processing steps depending on the specific image domain or application.

In conclusion, the integration of wavelet transforms and autoencoder networks presents a promising direction for future advancements in image denoising. This hybrid approach balances computational efficiency with high-quality denoising performance, making it suitable for a wide range of practical applications, including medical imaging, remote sensing, and consumer photography. Future work could explore the incorporation of other domain-specific knowledge, further enhancing the robustness and adaptability of this denoising framework across diverse imaging tasks.
